By the time he left Dynamo Kyiv, he had earned 70 caps and scored 26 goals for Ukraine.

In August 2017, Yarmolenko transferred to German club Borussia Dortmund for a reported fee of €25 million, signing a four-year contract. His time in the Bundesliga was marked by both promise and setbacks. He scored on his debut on August 19, 2017, in a 3–0 win over VfL Wolfsburg, but injuries limited his impact. Over two seasons, he made 39 appearances in all competitions, scoring 11 goals, including a memorable long-range strike against Bayern Munich in a 3–2 defeat on November 4, 2017. Despite flashes of brilliance, he struggled to secure a consistent starting role under managers Peter Bosz and later Lucien Favre.

In July 2018, Yarmolenko joined English club West Ham United for a fee of £17.5 million, signing a four-year deal. His Premier League career got off to a strong start, with two goals in his first three matches, including a stunning volley against Everton on September 16, 2018. However, his progress was derailed by a serious Achilles tendon injury in October 2018, which sidelined him for nearly eight months. He returned to action in May 2019 but struggled to regain his form in subsequent seasons. Despite this, he remained a key figure for Ukraine, captaining the team at UEFA Euro 2020 (held in 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic), where he scored two goals in four matches, including the opening goal in a 2–1 victory over the Netherlands.

After his contract with West Ham expired in June 2022, Yarmolenko signed with Al Ain FC in the UAE Pro League, joining the club on a free transfer. His move to the Middle East marked a new chapter, though his impact was limited by age and fitness concerns. He made 12 appearances for Al Ain, scoring three goals before leaving the club in January 2023. Later that year, he returned to Dynamo Kyiv on a short-term contract, reuniting with the club where he had risen to prominence. His second spell was brief, with limited playing time, but it allowed him to contribute to the team’s efforts in the Ukrainian Premier League.

By 2024, Yarmolenko had accumulated over 500 career appearances and more than 150 goals at club and international levels. Though his later years were marked by injuries and reduced playing time, his legacy as one of Ukraine’s greatest footballers remained secure. Known for his powerful left foot, technical skill, and leadership, he continued to be a respected figure in Ukrainian football, both as a player and a mentor to younger talents. His career, spanning nearly two decades, reflected both the highs of domestic and international success and the challenges of sustaining performance at the highest level.

title: Alexander Vovin
text:
Alexander Vladimirovich Vovin was born on January 27, 1961, in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg), Soviet Union, into an intellectual family with a strong academic background. His father, Vladimir Vovin, was a mathematician, and his mother, a philologist, fostered his early interest in languages. As a child, Vovin displayed an exceptional aptitude for linguistics, mastering multiple languages before enrolling at Leningrad State University in 1978. There, he studied under the renowned linguist Sergei Starostin, who specialized in historical and comparative linguistics. Vovin graduated in 1983 with a degree in Japanese philology, having already developed a deep fascination with the languages of East Asia, particularly those of the Altaic and Japonic families.

After completing his undergraduate studies, Vovin pursued postgraduate research at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, where he focused on the historical phonology of Japanese and its relationship to other languages. He earned his Candidate of Sciences degree (equivalent to a Ph.D.) in 1987 with a dissertation titled *"The Phonological System of Old Japanese and Its Reconstruction."* This work established his reputation as a meticulous scholar of early Japanese, challenging traditional views on the language’s development. During this period, he also began studying Korean and Ainu, two languages that would later become central to his research.

In 1990, Vovin emigrated to the United States, where he took a position as a visiting scholar at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. His move coincided with the collapse of the Soviet Union, which disrupted academic networks in Russia and created opportunities abroad. At Michigan, he worked closely with scholars such as Roy Andrew Miller, a leading figure in Altaic linguistics, and expanded his research into the comparative study of Japonic and Koreanic languages. In 1993, he joined the faculty of the University of Hawaii at Manoa as an assistant professor of Japanese and linguistics, where he would spend the next two decades. During his tenure, he published extensively on Old Japanese, Ainu, and the linguistic history of the Korean Peninsula, often challenging established theories.

One of Vovin’s most significant contributions was his work on the genetic classification of Japanese. In his 1993 monograph *"A Reconstruction of Proto-Ainu"* and his 2005 book *"A Descriptive and Comparative Grammar of Western Old Japanese,"* he argued that Japanese was not a member of the Altaic language family—a controversial stance at the time—but rather had deeper connections to the languages of the Pacific Rim, including Ainu. His 2009 paper *"Koreanic Loanwords in Old Japanese"* provided compelling evidence for early contact between Japanese and Korean speakers, reshaping scholarly understanding of the region’s linguistic history. Vovin’s approach combined rigorous philological analysis with comparative methods, often drawing on newly discovered historical texts and inscriptions.

Beyond Japanese, Vovin made substantial contributions to the study of Ainu, an endangered language indigenous to northern Japan. His 2008 work *"A Grammar of the Ainu Language"* was the first comprehensive modern grammar of the language, based on fieldwork and archival materials. He also published critical editions of classical Ainu texts, including the *"Ainu Folklore"* collection, which preserved oral traditions at risk of disappearing. His research on Korean included a 2010 monograph *"Koreanic Linguistics,"* where he proposed a new reconstruction of Middle Korean phonology, challenging earlier models by scholars like Samuel Martin.

In 2013, Vovin left the University of Hawaii to take up a position as Directeur d’Études at the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales (EHESS) in Paris, France. There, he continued his research on East Asian linguistics while mentoring a new generation of scholars. His later work included a 2017 study on the *"Man’yōshū,"* an 8th-century Japanese poetry anthology, where he analyzed its linguistic features to trace the evolution of Old Japanese. He also collaborated with archaeologists and historians to integrate linguistic evidence into broader discussions of East Asian prehistory.

Vovin’s career was marked by prolific output, with over 150 publications, including books, journal articles, and edited volumes. He was a frequent presenter at international conferences, often delivering keynote addresses on topics ranging from historical linguistics to language contact. Despite his rigorous scholarship, he was known for his humility and willingness to engage with junior researchers. His work earned him numerous accolades, including the Japan Foundation Award in 2012 and election to the Academia Europaea in 2015.

Alexander Vovin passed away on April 8, 2022, in Paris, at the age of 61, after a battle with cancer. His death was mourned by the global linguistics community, which recognized him as one of the foremost scholars of East Asian languages in the late 20th and early 21st centuries. His legacy endures in his publications, which remain foundational texts for students of Japanese, Korean, and Ainu, as well as in the many scholars he influenced through his teaching and mentorship.

title: Cobhams Asuquo
text:
Cobhams Emmanuel Asuquo was born on January 6, 1981, in Jos, Plateau State, Nigeria. From birth, he faced a significant challenge: he was born blind due to congenital glaucoma, a condition that affects the optic nerve. Despite this, his family, particularly his mother, Comfort Asuquo, played a crucial role in nurturing his talents and ensuring he received an education that accommodated his disability. He attended Pacelli School for the Blind in Lagos, a specialized institution that provided him with the tools to navigate life with visual impairment while fostering his intellectual and creative growth.

Asuquo’s passion for music emerged early. By the age of six, he had begun playing the piano, demonstrating an innate talent for music. His skills developed rapidly, and by his teenage years, he was already composing songs and performing in school events. After completing his secondary education, he enrolled at the University of Lagos, where he studied law. Though he pursued a legal education, his love for music remained unwavering, and he often balanced his academic responsibilities with musical pursuits. He graduated with a law degree in 2005, but his career path soon took a different turn.

In 2006, Asuquo’s professional music career began in earnest when he joined the music production team at QuestionMark Entertainment, a Lagos-based record label. His role as a producer and songwriter quickly gained recognition, and he worked with some of Nigeria’s most prominent artists. One of his earliest major contributions was producing the hit single "African Queen" for 2face Idibia (now 2Baba) in 2004, though the song’s success came after Asuquo had already established himself as a formidable talent. By 2007, he had produced tracks for artists like Banky W, Bez, and Omawumi, earning a reputation for his ability to blend Afrobeat, R&B, and soul into commercially successful music.

Asuquo’s breakthrough as a solo artist came in 2009 with the release of his debut album, *For Cobhams*. The album featured critically acclaimed tracks like "Ordinary People" and "We Plenty," which showcased his songwriting prowess and soulful vocals. The album was well-received, earning him nominations at the Headies Awards, Nigeria’s premier music awards ceremony, including Best R&B/Pop Album and Best Vocal Performance by a Male Artist. His success as an artist was complemented by his continued work as a producer, with credits on over 50 albums and singles by the mid-2010s.

Beyond music, Asuquo became an advocate for disability rights in Nigeria. In 2012, he founded the Cobhams Asuquo Foundation, a non-profit organization aimed at empowering people with disabilities through education, skills acquisition, and advocacy. The foundation has since partnered with various organizations, including the United Nations, to promote inclusivity and accessibility. His advocacy work earned him recognition, including the Nigerian National Honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in 2014, awarded by then-President Goodluck Jonathan for his contributions to music and social causes.

Asuquo’s career continued to flourish in the 2010s. In 2015, he released his second album, *The New Africa*, which featured collaborations with artists like Tiwa Savage and Sound Sultan. The album reinforced his status as a leading figure in Nigerian music, blending socially conscious lyrics with infectious melodies. He also ventured into entrepreneurship, co-founding Vintage Gray Media, a content creation and production company, in 2016. The company has since produced music videos, documentaries, and other multimedia projects, further expanding his influence in the entertainment industry.

In his personal life, Asuquo married Ojuolape Veronica in 2010, and the couple has three children. Despite his blindness, he has maintained an active lifestyle, often speaking about how his disability has shaped his perspective on creativity and resilience. He has also been open about the challenges of navigating Nigeria’s infrastructure, which often lacks accessibility for people with disabilities, using his platform to push for systemic change.

By the 2020s, Asuquo had cemented his legacy as one of Nigeria’s most versatile musicians and producers. He continued to release music, including the 2021 single "We Move," which addressed themes of perseverance and hope. His work has earned him numerous awards, including multiple Headies Awards, a Nigeria Entertainment Award, and a City People Entertainment Award. Beyond accolades, his impact is measured by his ability to inspire others, particularly those with disabilities, to pursue their dreams despite societal barriers.

As of 2024, Cobhams Asuquo remains an active figure in Nigeria’s music and advocacy scenes. His journey from a blind child in Jos to a celebrated musician and social advocate serves as a testament to his talent, determination, and commitment to using his platform for positive change. Whether through his music, his foundation, or his public speaking, he continues to break barriers and redefine what is possible for people with disabilities in Africa.

title: Thierry Henry
text:
Thierry Henry was born on August 17, 1977, in Les Ulis, a suburb of Paris, France. Raised in a working-class family, his father, Antoine, was from Guadeloupe, and his mother, Maryse, was from Martinique. From a young age, Henry displayed exceptional athletic ability, initially excelling in athletics before focusing on football. At the age of 13, he joined the youth academy of CO Les Ulis, a local club, where his talent quickly became evident. By 1992, he was scouted by AS Monaco, one of France’s top clubs, and joined their prestigious youth system.

Henry made his professional debut for AS Monaco on August 31, 1994, at the age of 17, in a Ligue 1 match against OGC Nice. Under the guidance of manager Arsène Wenger, he developed into a versatile forward, initially playing as a winger before transitioning into a striker. During his time at Monaco, Henry scored 20 goals in 105 league appearances and helped the club win the Ligue 1 title in the 1996-97 season. His performances earned him a call-up to the French national team, making his debut on October 11, 1997, in a 2-1 win over South Africa.

In January 1999, Henry transferred to Juventus for a fee of around £10.5 million. However, his time in Italy was short-lived, as he struggled to adapt to the defensive style of Serie A. After just eight months and three goals in 16 appearances, he was sold to Arsenal in August 1999 for £10.5 million, reuniting with Arsène Wenger. At Arsenal, Wenger converted Henry into a central striker, a role in which he would become one of the greatest players in Premier League history. During his eight-year spell at the club, Henry scored 228 goals in 377 appearances across all competitions, becoming Arsenal’s all-time leading scorer. He won two Premier League titles (2001-02 and 2003-04) and three FA Cups (2002, 2003, and 2005). The 2003-04 season was particularly historic, as Arsenal went unbeaten in the league, earning the nickname "The Invincibles." Henry was the league’s top scorer in 2001-02 (24 goals), 2003-04 (30 goals), 2004-05 (25 goals), and 2005-06 (27 goals). He also won the Premier League Golden Boot a record four times and was named the PFA Players’ Player of the Year twice (2003 and 2004).

On the international stage, Henry was a key figure in France’s golden era. He was part of the squad that won the 1998 FIFA World Cup on home soil, scoring three goals in the tournament, including two in the group stage against South Africa. He also played a crucial role in France’s victory at UEFA Euro 2000, where he scored three goals, including the winner in the semifinal against Portugal. Henry became France’s all-time leading scorer with 51 goals in 123 appearances, a record he held until Olivier Giroud surpassed it in 2022. He represented France in three World Cups (1998, 2002, and 2006) and three European Championships (2000, 2004, and 2008). His most memorable World Cup moment came in 2006, when France reached the final, though they lost to Italy on penalties. Henry’s assist for Zinedine Zidane’s goal in the final remains one of the tournament’s iconic moments.

In June 2007, Henry left Arsenal to join Barcelona for a fee of £16.1 million. At Barcelona, he formed a formidable attacking trio with Lionel Messi and Samuel Eto’o, helping the club achieve unprecedented success. During his three seasons at Barcelona, Henry scored 49 goals in 121 appearances and won six trophies, including the La Liga title in 2008-09 and the UEFA Champions League in 2009. His time in Spain was marked by his adaptability, often playing on the left wing to accommodate Messi’s central role. In July 2010, Henry signed with the New York Red Bulls in Major League Soccer (MLS), where he spent four and a half seasons. He scored 52 goals in 122 appearances and helped the team win the MLS Supporters’ Shield in 2013. He briefly returned to Arsenal on loan in February 2012, making four appearances and scoring one goal.

After retiring from professional football in December 2014, Henry transitioned into coaching. He began his managerial career as an assistant coach for the Belgium national team in 2016, working under Roberto Martínez. In October 2018, he was appointed head coach of Monaco, his first club, but his tenure was short and unsuccessful, lasting just three months. He later returned to MLS, becoming head coach of the Montreal Impact (now CF Montréal) in November 2019. Under his leadership, the team reached the playoffs in the 2020 season, but he left in February 2021 due to personal reasons. In 2023, he joined Sky Sports as a pundit, where he provides expert analysis on Premier League matches.

Beyond football, Henry has been involved in various charitable initiatives. He is a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador and has supported campaigns against racism and discrimination. In 2007, he launched the "Stand Up Speak Up" campaign to combat racism in football, partnering with Nike to produce wristbands that became a global symbol of anti-racism. Henry has also been recognized for his contributions to the sport, being inducted into the Premier League Hall of Fame in 2021 and the English Football Hall of Fame in 2022. He remains one of the most iconic and influential figures in football history, celebrated for his skill, leadership, and impact both on and off the pitch.

title: Gary Woodland
text:
Gary Woodland was born on May 21, 1984, in Topeka, Kansas, to parents Dan and Linda Woodland. Growing up in the small town of Shawnee, Kansas, he developed an early passion for sports, particularly basketball and baseball. However, it was golf that ultimately captured his interest. Woodland attended Shawnee Heights High School, where he excelled in multiple sports, but his golf skills began to stand out. By his senior year, he was named the Kansas Class 5A state golf champion in 2002, posting a two-day score of 142 at the Salina Municipal Golf Course.

After high school, Woodland enrolled at Washburn University in Topeka on a basketball scholarship, playing as a forward for the Ichabods during the 2002-03 season. However, his focus shifted back to golf, and he transferred to the University of Kansas in 2004 to join the Jayhawks’ golf team. Under coach Ross Randall, Woodland quickly became one of the team’s top players. In 2006, he earned All-Big 12 honors and helped Kansas reach the NCAA Championship, where they finished 13th. That same year, he turned professional at the age of 22, forgoing his final year of college eligibility.

Woodland’s early professional career was marked by struggles on smaller tours. He played on the Nationwide Tour (now the Korn Ferry Tour) in 2007 and 2008, with limited success. His breakthrough came in 2008 when he Monday-qualified for the U.S. Open at Torrey Pines, where he made the cut and finished tied for 48th, earning $52,000. This performance earned him conditional status on the PGA Tour for 2009, but he still spent much of the year grinding on the Nationwide Tour. In 2009, he secured his first professional victory at the Preferred Health Systems Wichita Open, a Nationwide Tour event, with a final-round 65 to win by one stroke. This win, along with consistent play, helped him finish 11th on the Nationwide Tour money list, earning his PGA Tour card for 2010.

Woodland’s first full season on the PGA Tour in 2010 was solid but unspectacular, with three top-10 finishes and $1.3 million in earnings. His first PGA Tour victory came on February 19, 2011, at the Transitions Championship in Palm Harbor, Florida. He shot a final-round 67 to win by one stroke over Webb Simpson and earn $936,000. This win propelled him into the top 50 of the Official World Golf Ranking and secured his status on the tour for the next several years. Over the next few seasons, Woodland remained a consistent performer, finishing in the top 50 on the money list each year from 2011 to 2015, with multiple top-10 finishes, including a tie for second at the 2013 Wells Fargo Championship.

His career reached new heights in 2018 when he won the Waste Management Phoenix Open, one of the PGA Tour’s most prestigious non-major events. He birdied three of the last four holes to shoot a final-round 67 and win by one stroke over Chez Reavie, earning $1.368 million. That year, he also recorded his best finish in a major at the PGA Championship, where he tied for sixth at Bellerive Country Club. However, his defining moment came on June 16, 2019, when he won his first major championship at the U.S. Open at Pebble Beach Golf Links. Woodland shot a final-round 69 to finish at 13-under par, three strokes ahead of two-time defending champion Brooks Koepka. His victory was highlighted by a clutch 30-foot birdie putt on the 17th hole and a masterful up-and-down from the rough on the 18th. The win earned him $2.25 million and a five-year exemption on the PGA Tour.

In the years following his U.S. Open victory, Woodland remained a competitive presence on the tour, though he struggled with injuries and inconsistent form. In 2020, he underwent surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right shoulder, which sidelined him for several months. He returned in 2021 but failed to regain his previous form, finishing outside the top 100 on the money list for the first time since 2010. Despite this, he continued to play at a high level in select events, recording a tie for fourth at the 2022 PGA Championship at Southern Hills.

Off the course, Woodland has been actively involved in charitable work, particularly through the Gary Woodland Foundation, which he established to support children’s health and wellness initiatives. He married his wife, Gabby, in 2013, and the couple has three children: Jaxson, born in 2015, and twins Jace and Jade, born in 2018. Woodland has also been open about his struggles with mental health, advocating for greater awareness and support within the golf community.

As of 2024, Woodland continues to compete on the PGA Tour, though his focus has shifted toward maintaining his game while balancing family life. While he has not added to his four PGA Tour victories since 2019, his legacy as a major champion and one of the most powerful drivers in golf history remains secure. His U.S. Open triumph at Pebble Beach stands as the pinnacle of his career, a moment that solidified his place among the game’s elite.

title: Vicente Guerrero
text:
Vicente Guerrero was born on August 10, 1782, in Tixtla, a small town in what is now the state of Guerrero, Mexico. His parents were Pedro Guerrero, a mestizo of African and Indigenous descent, and María de Guadalupe Saldaña, an Indigenous woman. The family belonged to the lower social strata, and Guerrero grew up in a rural environment, working as a muleteer and merchant in his youth. His early exposure to the struggles of Mexico’s marginalized populations shaped his later revolutionary ideals.

Guerrero’s military career began in 1810 when he joined the insurgent forces led by José María Morelos during Mexico’s War of Independence from Spain. By 1812, he had risen to the rank of captain under Morelos, participating in key battles such as the Siege of Cuautla (February–May 1812) and the capture of Oaxaca in November 1812. After Morelos was captured and executed in 1815, Guerrero continued the fight as a guerrilla leader in southern Mexico, operating primarily in the mountainous regions of what is now Guerrero and Oaxaca. Despite the collapse of the insurgency’s central leadership, he maintained resistance with a small but determined force, earning a reputation for resilience.

In 1821, Guerrero played a pivotal role in the final phase of the independence movement. After initially rejecting offers to join Agustín de Iturbide’s Plan of Iguala—a proposal for Mexican independence under a constitutional monarchy—Guerrero eventually agreed to an alliance in February 1821. Their combined forces, known as the Army of the Three Guarantees (religion, independence, and union), secured Mexico’s independence from Spain. The Treaty of Córdoba, signed on August 24, 1821, formalized Mexico’s sovereignty, and Guerrero became one of the new nation’s most prominent military leaders.

Following independence, Guerrero remained a key political figure. In 1823, he supported the overthrow of Iturbide’s short-lived empire and the establishment of a republic. He served as a military commander in southern Mexico and later as governor of the state of Puebla in 1824. In 1828, he ran for president as the candidate of the liberal Yorkino faction, opposing the conservative candidate Manuel Gómez Pedraza. When Gómez Pedraza won the election, Guerrero’s supporters, led by Antonio López de Santa Anna, staged a coup. Guerrero assumed the presidency on April 1, 1829, becoming Mexico’s second president and the first of African descent.

As president, Guerrero implemented progressive policies, including the abolition of slavery on September 16, 1829, fulfilling a promise made during the independence struggle. He also sought to reduce the political influence of the Catholic Church and the military, measures that alienated conservative elites. His presidency was short-lived; in December 1829, conservative forces led by Vice President Anastasio Bustamante launched a rebellion. Guerrero left Mexico City in January 1830 to suppress the uprising but was betrayed by one of his own officers, José Gabriel de Armijo, who defected to Bustamante. Guerrero retreated to the south, where he continued resistance as a guerrilla leader.

In early 1831, Guerrero was lured onto a ship under the pretense of negotiations and captured by Italian mercenary Francisco Picaluga, who had been bribed by Bustamante’s government. He was taken to Cuilápam, Oaxaca, where a military tribunal sentenced him to death. On February 14, 1831, at the age of 48, Guerrero was executed by firing squad. His death was widely mourned, and he became a martyr for Mexico’s liberal and progressive movements. In 1849, the state of Guerrero was named in his honor, cementing his legacy as one of Mexico’s most important independence leaders and a symbol of resistance against oppression.

title: Danny Faure
text:
Danny Faure was born on May 8, 1962, in Kilembe, Uganda, to Seychellois parents who were working in the East African country at the time. His family returned to Seychelles when he was still a young child, settling on the island of Mahé, where Faure grew up. He attended local schools before pursuing higher education abroad. In 1983, he enrolled at the University of Havana in Cuba, where he studied political science, graduating in 1987. His time in Cuba was formative, exposing him to socialist ideologies that would later influence his political career in Seychelles.

Upon returning to Seychelles, Faure joined the public sector, beginning his career in the Ministry of Education in 1988. His early roles involved administrative and policy work, and he quickly gained a reputation for competence and dedication. By 1993, he had risen to the position of Principal Secretary for Education, a role he held until 1998. During this period, Seychelles was undergoing political reforms, transitioning from a one-party state under President France-Albert René to a multi-party democracy. Faure’s work in education aligned with the government’s emphasis on expanding access to schooling, a priority for the ruling Seychelles People’s Progressive Front (SPPF), later renamed United Seychelles.

In 1998, Faure was appointed Minister of Education, a position he held for eight years until 2006. His tenure was marked by efforts to modernize the education system, including the introduction of vocational training programs and the expansion of tertiary education opportunities. In 2004, he oversaw the establishment of the University of Seychelles, the country’s first national university, which opened its doors in September of that year. His leadership in education earned him respect across the political spectrum, and he became one of the most prominent figures in President René’s administration.

Faure’s political career advanced further in 2006 when President James Michel, who had succeeded René in 2004, appointed him Minister of Finance. This role was critical as Seychelles faced economic challenges, including high public debt and reliance on foreign aid. Faure played a key role in negotiating a $26 million standby loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 2008, which helped stabilize the country’s economy. His financial management was widely praised, and in 2010, he was appointed Minister of Finance, Trade, and Investment, a position he held until 2016.

In 2010, Faure also became Vice President of Seychelles, serving under President Michel. This dual role solidified his position as the second-most powerful figure in the government. As Vice President, he oversaw key portfolios, including defense, youth, and sports, while continuing to manage economic policies. His leadership was tested in 2013 when Seychelles faced a severe foreign exchange crisis, prompting another IMF intervention. Faure’s negotiations secured a $17.6 million loan, which helped restore economic stability.

On October 16, 2016, Faure became President of Seychelles following the resignation of James Michel, who stepped down mid-term. Faure’s presidency was marked by efforts to maintain economic stability and promote sustainable development. One of his early achievements was the successful renegotiation of Seychelles’ debt with the Paris Club in 2017, reducing the country’s debt burden by $21 million. He also prioritized environmental conservation, expanding marine protected areas to cover 30% of Seychelles’ exclusive economic zone by 2020, a significant increase from previous levels.

Faure’s presidency faced challenges, including the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, which devastated Seychelles’ tourism-dependent economy. In response, his government implemented strict public health measures and secured financial assistance from international partners, including a $10 million loan from the IMF in 2020. Despite these efforts, his administration struggled with public dissatisfaction over economic hardships, leading to his defeat in the October 2020 presidential election. He lost to Wavel Ramkalawan, the leader of the opposition Linyon Demokratik Seselwa (LDS), who won with 54.9% of the vote compared to Faure’s 43.5%.

After leaving office, Faure remained active in public life, though he largely stepped back from frontline politics. In 2021, he was appointed as a special envoy for the African Union, focusing on climate change and ocean governance. He also became a senior advisor to the Pew Bertarelli Ocean Legacy Project, advocating for marine conservation in the Indian Ocean. Faure continues to reside in Seychelles, where he occasionally speaks on national issues, though he has not sought a return to elected office. His career reflects a blend of technocratic expertise and political leadership, shaping Seychelles’ development over three decades.

title: Ilhan Omar
text:
Ilhan Omar was born on October 4, 1982, in Mogadishu, Somalia, the youngest of seven siblings in a middle-class family. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, was a teacher and later worked for the Somali government, while her mother, Fadhuma Abukar Haji Hussein, died when Ilhan was just two years old. Raised primarily by her father and grandfather, she spent her early childhood in Somalia before the outbreak of civil war in 1991 forced her family to flee. They spent four years in a refugee camp in Dadaab, Kenya, where conditions were harsh, with limited food and shelter. In 1995, at the age of 12, Omar and her family were granted asylum in the United States, settling in Arlington, Virginia, before eventually moving to Minneapolis, Minnesota, in 1997.

Omar attended Edison High School in Minneapolis, where she became involved in student government and community activism. After graduating in 2001, she enrolled at North Dakota State University, earning a bachelor’s degree in political science and international studies in 2011. During her college years, she worked as a community nutrition educator at the University of Minnesota and later as a child nutrition outreach coordinator for the Minnesota Department of Education. In 2002, at the age of 19, she married Ahmed Hirsi, with whom she had three children: Isra Hirsi (born 2002), Ilwad Hirsi (born 2005), and Adnan Hirsi (born 2011). The couple separated in 2008 but later reconciled.

Omar’s political career began in earnest in 2012 when she worked as a campaign manager for Kari Dziedzic’s Minnesota State Senate campaign. That same year, she became a senior policy aide for Minneapolis City Council member Andrew Johnson. In 2013, she married Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, though the legality of this marriage later became a subject of controversy. She and Hirsi divorced in 2017, and she legally married Hirsi again in 2018. Omar’s early activism focused on issues such as affordable housing, healthcare access, and immigrant rights, which she pursued through her work with the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL) and various nonprofit organizations.

In 2016, Omar made history by winning the Minnesota House of Representatives District 60B primary, defeating 44-year incumbent Phyllis Kahn and Mohamud Noor in a three-way race. She went on to win the general election unopposed, becoming the first Somali-American legislator in the United States. During her tenure in the Minnesota House, which lasted from January 3, 2017, to January 3, 2019, she championed progressive policies, including a $15 minimum wage, tuition-free college, and criminal justice reform. She also co-authored a bill to ban private prisons in Minnesota, though it did not pass.

In 2018, Omar ran for the U.S. House of Representatives in Minnesota’s 5th congressional district, which includes Minneapolis and surrounding areas. She won the DFL primary with 48.2% of the vote in a crowded field of five candidates, including longtime state representative Margaret Anderson Kelliher. In the general election, she defeated Republican Jennifer Zielinski with 78.0% of the vote, becoming one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress, alongside Rashida Tlaib of Michigan. She was also the first Somali-American and the first naturalized citizen from Africa elected to the U.S. House.

As a member of Congress, Omar has been a vocal advocate for progressive causes, including Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and student debt cancellation. She serves on the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and the House Committee on Education and Labor. In 2019, she introduced the No Ban Act, legislation aimed at reversing former President Donald Trump’s travel ban targeting majority-Muslim countries. The bill passed the House in 2020 but was not taken up by the Senate. Omar has also been a prominent critic of U.S. foreign policy, particularly regarding Israel and Palestine, which has drawn both praise and controversy. In 2021, she was appointed as whip for the Congressional Progressive Caucus, a role in which she helps coordinate legislative strategy among progressive members.

Omar has faced significant backlash for her outspoken views, including accusations of antisemitism for her criticism of the Israeli government and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). In 2019, the House passed a resolution condemning antisemitism, Islamophobia, and other forms of bigotry, which was widely seen as a rebuke of Omar’s remarks, though it did not name her directly. Despite this, she has remained a polarizing figure, admired by progressives for her advocacy on behalf of marginalized communities and criticized by opponents for her foreign policy stances.

In 2020, Omar faced a primary challenge from Antone Melton-Meaux, a moderate Democrat who raised over $4 million in an attempt to unseat her. However, she won the primary with 57.4% of the vote and went on to secure re-election in the general election with 64.3% of the vote. In 2022, she faced another primary challenge, this time from Don Samuels, a former Minneapolis City Council member, but again won with 50.3% of the vote. As of 2024, Omar continues to serve in Congress, where she remains a leading voice for progressive policies and a frequent target of political attacks. She lives in Minneapolis with her husband, Ahmed Hirsi, and their three children.

title: Joey Jordison
text:
Joey Jordison, born Nathan Jonas Jordison on April 26, 1975, in Des Moines, Iowa, was a renowned American musician best known as the drummer and co-founder of the heavy metal band Slipknot. Jordison grew up in a working-class family, the youngest of three children, with his father, Steve Jordison, working as a mechanic and his mother, Jackie Jordison, as a nurse. From an early age, Jordison displayed a deep passion for music, particularly drumming. He received his first drum kit at the age of eight and began playing in local bands during his teenage years. His early influences included bands like Kiss, Black Sabbath, and Metallica, which shaped his aggressive and precise drumming style.

Jordison’s professional music career began in earnest in 1995 when he co-founded Slipknot alongside bassist Paul Gray and percussionist Shawn Crahan. The band quickly gained a reputation for their intense live performances and masked personas, with Jordison adopting the number 1 as his stage identity. Slipknot’s self-titled debut album, released on June 29, 1999, catapulted them to international fame, selling over 2 million copies in the U.S. alone and earning platinum certification. Jordison’s drumming on tracks like "Spit It Out" and "Wait and Bleed" showcased his technical skill and speed, earning him widespread acclaim. The band’s follow-up album, *Iowa* (2001), debuted at number 3 on the Billboard 200 and solidified their status as one of the most influential metal bands of the 2000s.

Beyond Slipknot, Jordison was involved in numerous side projects. In 2001, he joined the horror-themed metal supergroup Murderdolls, where he played guitar under the name "Number One." The band released their debut album, *Beyond the Valley of the Murderdolls*, in August 2002, which featured a mix of glam metal and punk influences. Jordison also collaborated with other artists, including Rob Zombie, for whom he played drums on the 2001 album *The Sinister Urge* and during live tours. Additionally, he was a member of the short-lived band Scar the Martyr, formed in 2013, which released one self-titled album before disbanding in 2016.

Jordison’s contributions to music were widely recognized. In 2010, *Rhythm Magazine* named him the best drummer of the past 25 years in a reader’s poll, and in 2013, he was ranked the second-best drummer of all time by *Loudwire*. His work with Slipknot earned the band a Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance in 2006 for the song "Before I Forget." Jordison was also known for his custom drum kits, including a signature Pearl Reference Pure drum set, which featured a unique black and silver finish and was designed to withstand the demands of his high-energy performances.

Despite his success, Jordison’s later years were marked by personal and professional challenges. In December 2013, Slipknot announced that Jordison had left the band, citing personal reasons. Jordison later revealed in a 2016 interview that he had been unknowingly suffering from transverse myelitis, a rare neurological disease that caused inflammation in his spinal cord, leading to severe mobility issues. The condition had affected his ability to play drums, forcing him to step away from music temporarily. After undergoing treatment, Jordison gradually regained his strength and returned to performing, joining the band Sinsaenum in 2016, a blackened death metal project that released two albums, *Echoes of the Tortured* (2016) and *Repulsion for Humanity* (2018).

Jordison’s final years were spent touring and recording with Sinsaenum, as well as making occasional appearances at music festivals. On July 26, 2021, Jordison passed away in his sleep at the age of 46. The cause of death was later revealed to be complications from transverse myelitis. His death was met with an outpouring of tributes from fans and fellow musicians, who remembered him as one of the most influential drummers in modern metal. Jordison’s legacy endures through his groundbreaking work with Slipknot and his contributions to the broader metal community, cementing his place as a defining figure in heavy music.

title: Nelson Mandela
text:
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was born on July 18, 1918, in the small village of Mvezo, in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. His father, Gadla Henry Mphakanyiswa, was a local chief and counselor to the Thembu royal family, while his mother, Nosekeni Fanny, was the third of his father’s four wives. Mandela was given the name Rolihlahla, which colloquially means "troublemaker" in Xhosa, a name that would later reflect his defiance against injustice. At the age of seven, he became the first in his family to attend school, where a Methodist teacher gave him the English name "Nelson." When Mandela was nine, his father died of lung disease, and he was placed under the guardianship of Jongintaba Dalindyebo, the acting regent of the Thembu people, who groomed him for leadership.

Mandela attended Clarkebury Boarding Institute and later Healdtown, a Wesleyan secondary school, where he excelled in academics and athletics. In 1939, he enrolled at the University of Fort Hare, the only Western-style higher education institution for Black South Africans at the time. There, he studied law and became involved in student politics, joining the Student Representative Council. After being expelled in 1940 for participating in a boycott against the university’s policies, he fled to Johannesburg to avoid an arranged marriage. In Johannesburg, he worked as a mine security officer and completed his BA through the University of South Africa via correspondence in 1943. He then began studying law at the University of the Witwatersrand, where he met future anti-apartheid activists Walter Sisulu and Oliver Tambo.

Mandela joined the African National Congress (ANC) in 1944, a pivotal moment in his political career. That same year, he co-founded the ANC Youth League with Sisulu, Tambo, and others, advocating for a more militant approach to resisting apartheid, South Africa’s system of institutionalized racial segregation. In 1948, the National Party, which promoted apartheid, came to power, and Mandela’s activism intensified. He played a key role in the 1952 Defiance Campaign, a nonviolent protest against apartheid laws that led to his first arrest. In 1955, he helped draft the Freedom Charter, a document outlining the ANC’s vision for a democratic, non-racial South Africa. However, the government responded with repression, charging Mandela and 155 others with treason in 1956. After a five-year trial, all defendants were acquitted in 1961.

By the early 1960s, Mandela had concluded that nonviolent resistance was ineffective against the apartheid regime. In 1961, he co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe ("Spear of the Nation"), the ANC’s armed wing, and became its commander-in-chief. On August 5, 1962, he was arrested after 17 months in hiding and sentenced to five years in prison for inciting workers’ strikes and leaving the country illegally. While serving this sentence, he was charged with sabotage and conspiracy in the Rivonia Trial, named after the Johannesburg suburb where ANC leaders were arrested in 1963. On June 12, 1964, Mandela and seven others were sentenced to life imprisonment. He spent the next 27 years in prison, primarily on Robben Island, where he performed hard labor in a lime quarry and was allowed only one visitor and one letter every six months.

Despite his imprisonment, Mandela became a global symbol of resistance to apartheid. International pressure mounted, and in 1985, President P.W. Botha offered him conditional release if he renounced violence, which Mandela refused. His imprisonment ended on February 11, 1990, when President F.W. de Klerk, under growing domestic and international pressure, announced his release. Mandela immediately resumed his leadership of the ANC, which had been unbanned the same day. Over the next four years, he negotiated with the government to dismantle apartheid, culminating in South Africa’s first democratic elections in April 1994. The ANC won 62.6% of the vote, and on May 10, 1994, Mandela was inaugurated as South Africa’s first Black president, serving a single term until 1999.

As president, Mandela focused on national reconciliation, establishing the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 1995 to investigate apartheid-era crimes. He also implemented policies to address poverty and inequality, including the Reconstruction and Development Programme, which built over one million houses and provided access to water and electricity for millions. Despite his global stature, Mandela remained humble, donating a third of his presidential salary to the Nelson Mandela Children’s Fund, which he founded in 1995. After leaving office, he continued his activism, advocating for HIV/AIDS awareness, education, and peace. In 2004, at the age of 85, he announced his retirement from public life, though he remained involved in charitable work.

Mandela’s later years were marked by health struggles, including respiratory infections likely linked to the tuberculosis he contracted during his imprisonment. He was hospitalized multiple times, including in 2011, 2012, and 2013. On December 5, 2013, Mandela died at his home in Johannesburg at the age of 95, surrounded by family. His death prompted an outpouring of global tributes, and he was given a state funeral in Qunu, his ancestral village, on December 15, 2013. Mandela’s legacy endures through his writings, including his autobiography *Long Walk to Freedom* (1994), and the countless institutions bearing his name, such as the Nelson Mandela Foundation, which continues his work in social justice. He remains one of the most revered figures of the 20th century, a symbol of resilience, forgiveness, and the fight for equality.

title: Ayman al-Zawahiri
text:
Ayman al-Zawahiri was born on June 19, 1951, in the affluent Maadi district of Cairo, Egypt, into a prominent and educated family. His father, Mohammed Rabie al-Zawahiri, was a professor of pharmacology at Cairo University, while his mother, Umayma Azzam, came from a politically influential family; her father, Abdel Wahab Azzam, was a diplomat and the first secretary-general of the Arab League. Al-Zawahiri grew up in a household that valued both religious piety and intellectual rigor, though his family was not overtly radical. He attended Cairo University’s medical school, graduating in 1974 with a degree in surgery and later earning a master’s degree in surgery in 1978. During his university years, he became deeply involved in Islamic activism, influenced by the writings of Sayyid Qutb, an Egyptian Islamist theorist executed by the government in 1966.

Al-Zawahiri’s radicalization intensified in the late 1960s and early 1970s as he joined the Egyptian Islamic Jihad (EIJ), a militant group dedicated to overthrowing the Egyptian government and establishing an Islamic state. He was arrested in 1981 following the assassination of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat by Islamic extremists on October 6 of that year. Though al-Zawahiri was not directly involved in the assassination, he was imprisoned for three years on charges of illegal arms possession. During his incarceration, he was reportedly tortured, an experience that further hardened his resolve against secular governments. After his release in 1984, he traveled to Saudi Arabia and later to Peshawar, Pakistan, where he worked as a surgeon treating wounded mujahideen fighters during the Soviet-Afghan War (1979–1989). It was in Peshawar that he first met Osama bin Laden, who was then a rising figure in the Afghan resistance.

By the late 1980s, al-Zawahiri had become a key leader in the EIJ, which carried out a series of attacks in Egypt, including the 1995 bombing of the Egyptian Embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan, that killed 16 people. In 1998, he formally merged the EIJ with bin Laden’s al-Qaeda, becoming bin Laden’s second-in-command and the group’s chief ideologue. Al-Zawahiri played a central role in planning the August 7, 1998, bombings of the U.S. embassies in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, which killed 224 people and injured over 4,500. The attacks marked al-Qaeda’s emergence as a global terrorist threat and led to the U.S. designating al-Zawahiri as one of the FBI’s Most Wanted Terrorists, with a $25 million reward for his capture.

Following the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States, al-Zawahiri became one of the most sought-after figures in the world. He appeared in numerous al-Qaeda propaganda videos, issuing threats against the U.S. and its allies. In 2003, he was reportedly involved in the planning of the Riyadh compound bombings in Saudi Arabia, which killed 35 people. Despite the U.S. invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and the subsequent dismantling of al-Qaeda’s safe havens, al-Zawahiri evaded capture, likely hiding in the tribal regions along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. He succeeded bin Laden as the leader of al-Qaeda after bin Laden was killed by U.S. Navy SEALs in Abbottabad, Pakistan, on May 2, 2011.

As al-Qaeda’s leader, al-Zawahiri oversaw the group’s adaptation to a more decentralized model, with affiliates like al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) gaining prominence. He continued to release audio and video messages, including a 2014 statement endorsing the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) before its split from al-Qaeda. However, his leadership was marked by al-Qaeda’s declining influence relative to ISIS, which attracted more recruits and carried out larger-scale attacks. On July 31, 2022, al-Zawahiri was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Kabul, Afghanistan, where he had reportedly been living under Taliban protection since the group’s return to power in August 2021. The strike, conducted by the CIA, used Hellfire missiles and occurred on a balcony of a safe house in the Sherpur neighborhood, killing al-Zawahiri instantly without causing other casualties. His death marked the end of a four-decade career as one of the world’s most notorious terrorists.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez, born on February 27, 1888, in Bogotá, Colombia, was a prominent garden designer whose work left a lasting impact on landscape architecture in the United States. His early life was marked by a blend of cultural influences, as his father, General Eustorgio Salgar, served as Colombia’s president from 1870 to 1872, and his mother, María Josefa Suárez, came from a distinguished family. Suarez spent his formative years in Colombia before moving to Europe at the age of 12, where he was exposed to the grand gardens of France and Italy, which would later shape his design philosophy.

Suarez studied architecture and horticulture in Paris, attending the École des Beaux-Arts, where he developed a deep appreciation for classical garden design. By 1910, he had relocated to the United States, settling in New York City. His early career involved collaborations with prominent architects, including Carrère and Hastings, who were known for their work on grand estates. Suarez’s first major commission came in 1914 when he was hired to design the gardens for the estate of James Deering in Miami, Florida. This project, known as Villa Vizcaya, became one of his most celebrated works. Over the next decade, Suarez meticulously crafted the estate’s 10 acres of formal gardens, integrating Italian Renaissance and Baroque elements with tropical flora, resulting in a harmonious blend of European elegance and subtropical beauty.

Throughout the 1920s and 1930s, Suarez’s reputation grew as he worked on numerous high-profile projects. In 1922, he designed the gardens for the estate of Charles Deering in Cutler, Florida, known as the Deering Estate, which featured a mix of formal and naturalistic landscapes. His work on the estate of William Randolph Hearst in San Simeon, California, beginning in 1920, further solidified his standing as a master of large-scale garden design. Suarez collaborated with architect Julia Morgan on this project, creating terraced gardens, pools, and pathways that complemented Hearst’s sprawling estate, which covered over 250,000 acres.

Suarez’s design approach was characterized by his ability to adapt classical European styles to the American landscape, often incorporating native plants and local materials. His gardens were known for their symmetry, axial layouts, and careful attention to detail, as seen in his work on the estate of John D. Rockefeller Jr. in Pocantico Hills, New York, where he designed the gardens for Kykuit, the family’s historic home. The project, completed in the 1930s, featured terraces, fountains, and sculptures, all arranged in a formal, geometric pattern that reflected Suarez’s training in Beaux-Arts principles.

In addition to his private commissions, Suarez contributed to public projects, including the design of the gardens for the New York Botanical Garden’s Conservatory Lawn in the 1930s. His work there demonstrated his ability to create serene, contemplative spaces that blended seamlessly with their surroundings. Despite the economic challenges of the Great Depression, Suarez continued to receive commissions, though on a smaller scale, as many of his wealthy clients scaled back their projects.

Suarez’s later years were marked by a shift toward teaching and mentoring. In the 1940s, he became a lecturer at Columbia University’s School of Architecture, where he shared his expertise in landscape design with a new generation of students. He also wrote articles for architectural and horticultural publications, advocating for the preservation of historic gardens and the integration of sustainable practices in landscape design. His final major project was the redesign of the gardens at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens in Miami, which he revisited in the 1950s to restore and enhance the original designs he had created decades earlier.

Diego Suarez passed away on October 10, 1974, in New York City, at the age of 86. His legacy endures through the many gardens he designed, which remain admired for their beauty and innovation. Villa Vizcaya, now a National Historic Landmark, stands as a testament to his vision, attracting thousands of visitors each year. Suarez’s work bridged the gap between European tradition and American innovation, leaving an indelible mark on the field of landscape architecture. His contributions were recognized posthumously, including his induction into the American Society of Landscape Architects’ Council of Fellows in 1975, cementing his place as one of the most influential garden designers of the 20th century.

title: Muhammad Qutb
text:
Muhammad Qutb was born on April 26, 1919, in the village of Musha, near the city of Asyut in Upper Egypt. He was the younger brother of Sayyid Qutb, one of the most influential Islamic thinkers of the 20th century. Their father, Qutb Ibrahim, was a landowner and a respected figure in the community, while their mother, Fatima Husayn, came from a family with strong religious ties. Muhammad grew up in a devout Muslim household, where Islamic teachings and values were deeply ingrained. He received his early education in local schools before moving to Cairo to pursue higher studies.

In Cairo, Muhammad Qutb enrolled at Cairo University, where he studied literature and education. He graduated in 1940 with a degree in Arabic language and literature, after which he began his career as a teacher. His first teaching position was at a secondary school in Asyut, where he worked from 1941 to 1945. During this period, he also became increasingly involved in Islamic activism, influenced by his brother Sayyid Qutb, who was already emerging as a prominent Islamic scholar and writer. Muhammad’s early writings reflected his growing interest in Islamic revivalism, particularly in response to the secular and Westernizing trends in Egyptian society under the monarchy.

By the late 1940s, Muhammad Qutb had become a vocal critic of the Egyptian government and its alignment with Western powers. In 1948, he joined the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamic organization founded by Hassan al-Banna in 1928, which advocated for the establishment of an Islamic state governed by Sharia law. His association with the Brotherhood deepened after the assassination of al-Banna in 1949, an event that radicalized many of its members, including Sayyid Qutb. Muhammad’s role in the organization was primarily intellectual; he contributed articles to the Brotherhood’s publications, such as *Al-Da’wa* and *Al-Ikhwan al-Muslimeen*, where he expounded on themes of Islamic governance, social justice, and resistance to colonialism.

In 1954, the Egyptian government, under President Gamal Abdel Nasser, launched a brutal crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood, accusing it of attempting to assassinate Nasser. Thousands of members were arrested, including both Sayyid and Muhammad Qutb. While Sayyid was sentenced to death and executed in 1966, Muhammad was imprisoned for nearly a decade. He was held in various detention camps, including the infamous Tura Prison, where he endured harsh conditions alongside other Brotherhood members. Despite the repression, Muhammad continued to write, producing several books during his imprisonment, including *Islam: The Misunderstood Religion* (1960) and *Our Contemporary Civilization* (1963), which critiqued Western materialism and secularism while advocating for an Islamic alternative.

After his release in 1964, Muhammad Qutb was placed under house arrest and closely monitored by the Egyptian authorities. However, his reputation as an Islamic scholar had grown, and he was invited to teach in Saudi Arabia, where he relocated in 1965. He joined the faculty of King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah, where he taught Islamic studies and became a mentor to a new generation of Islamic thinkers, including Osama bin Laden, who attended the university in the late 1970s. Qutb’s lectures and writings during this period emphasized the concept of *jahiliyyah* (the state of ignorance of divine guidance) and the necessity of Islamic revolution, ideas that had been central to his brother’s work.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Muhammad Qutb expanded his influence through his writings and public lectures. He published numerous books, including *Islam and the Challenges of the Twentieth Century* (1979) and *The Future of Islam in the World* (1984), which addressed the perceived moral decline of Muslim societies and the need for Islamic revival. His works were widely read in the Arab world and beyond, particularly among Islamist movements. He also traveled extensively, delivering lectures in countries such as Pakistan, Malaysia, and the United States, where he engaged with Muslim communities and intellectuals.

Despite his global influence, Muhammad Qutb remained a controversial figure. His uncompromising stance on Islamic governance and his opposition to secularism drew criticism from both Western scholars and moderate Muslims. However, he was also respected for his intellectual rigor and his commitment to Islamic principles. In his later years, he continued to teach and write, residing primarily in Saudi Arabia. He passed away on April 4, 2014, in Mecca at the age of 94. His legacy endures through his extensive body of work, which continues to shape Islamic thought and activism in the 21st century.

title: Ivan Perišić
text:
Ivan Perišić was born on February 2, 1989, in Split, Croatia, a coastal city known for its footballing tradition. Growing up in the nearby town of Omiš, he began playing football at a young age, joining the youth academy of Hajduk Split, one of Croatia’s most storied clubs, at the age of 10 in 1999. His talent was evident early on, and by 2006, at just 17, he moved to France to join the youth system of FC Sochaux-Montbéliard, a club with a strong reputation for developing young players. This transition marked the beginning of his professional journey in European football.

Perišić made his professional debut for Sochaux’s senior team on August 16, 2008, in a Ligue 1 match against Auxerre, coming on as a substitute in a 1-0 defeat. However, he struggled to secure regular playing time and was loaned to Belgian club KSV Roeselare for the 2009-10 season to gain experience. There, he scored 5 goals in 22 appearances, catching the attention of Club Brugge, which signed him permanently in August 2010 for a reported fee of €250,000. His breakthrough came during the 2010-11 season, where he became a key player, scoring 22 goals in 37 league matches and winning the Belgian Pro League’s top scorer award. His performances earned him a move to Borussia Dortmund in May 2011 for a fee of around €5 million.

At Dortmund, Perišić joined a team on the rise under manager Jürgen Klopp. He made his Bundesliga debut on August 5, 2011, in a 3-1 win over Hamburger SV, and quickly became a versatile attacking option, contributing 7 goals and 8 assists in his first season. His most memorable moment came in the 2011-12 campaign when he scored the winning goal in a 1-0 victory over Bayern Munich in the DFB-Pokal final on May 12, 2012, helping Dortmund secure the domestic double. Despite his success, he was sold to VfL Wolfsburg in January 2013 for €8 million, where he spent two and a half seasons, scoring 18 goals in 67 league appearances and winning the DFB-Pokal again in 2015, this time as a starter in the final against Borussia Dortmund.

In July 2015, Perišić joined Inter Milan for a reported fee of €16 million, marking the beginning of his time in Serie A. Over six seasons, he became a reliable winger, scoring 40 goals in 164 league appearances. His most productive season came in 2019-20 under Antonio Conte, where he scored 8 goals and provided 6 assists, helping Inter finish second in the league. However, his relationship with Conte soured, leading to a loan move to Bayern Munich in August 2019. There, he won the Bundesliga and the UEFA Champions League, scoring in the 2020 UEFA Super Cup against Sevilla. After returning to Inter, he played a crucial role in their 2020-21 Serie A title-winning campaign, contributing 4 goals and 9 assists.

On the international stage, Perišić made his debut for the Croatian national team on March 26, 2011, in a 2-0 Euro 2012 qualifier win over Georgia. He quickly became a key player, representing Croatia at the 2012, 2016, and 2020 UEFA European Championships, as well as the 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups. His most notable performances came in the 2018 World Cup, where he scored 3 goals, including the equalizer in the final against France, and provided an assist in the 2-1 semi-final victory over England. Croatia finished as runners-up, and Perišić’s contributions earned him widespread recognition.

In August 2022, Perišić left Inter Milan to join Tottenham Hotspur on a free transfer, signing a two-year contract. He made his Premier League debut on August 6, 2022, in a 4-1 win over Southampton, and scored his first goal for the club in a 2-0 victory over Brighton & Hove Albion on October 1. Despite injuries limiting his impact, he remained a valuable squad player. Off the field, Perišić has been involved in charitable work, including donations to hospitals and youth football programs in Croatia. As of 2024, he continues to play for Tottenham, though his role has diminished with age. His career, spanning over a decade in top European leagues, reflects his adaptability, work ethic, and enduring quality as a footballer.

title: Daniel Alexander Cameron
text:
Daniel Alexander Cameron was born on June 14, 1908, in Sydney, Nova Scotia, a coastal town in Cape Breton Island, Canada. His parents, Alexander Cameron and Mary MacLeod, were of Scottish descent, reflecting the strong Gaelic heritage of the region. The family lived in a modest working-class neighborhood, where his father worked as a coal miner, a common occupation in the industrialized area. Cameron was the youngest of five children, and his early years were shaped by the economic struggles of the time, particularly during the post-World War I recession.

Cameron attended local public schools, where he demonstrated an aptitude for academics and public speaking. After completing his secondary education at Sydney Academy in 1926, he enrolled at St. Francis Xavier University in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, on a scholarship. There, he studied economics and political science, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1930. His education was influenced by the Antigonish Movement, a cooperative economic initiative that sought to alleviate poverty through adult education and community development, which left a lasting impression on his political views.

Upon graduation, Cameron briefly worked as a high school teacher in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, from 1930 to 1932, before pursuing further studies at the University of Toronto. He earned a Master of Arts degree in economics in 1934, writing a thesis on labor relations in the coal industry. That same year, he joined the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (CCF), Canada’s first major socialist party, which later evolved into the New Democratic Party (NDP). His political activism began in earnest during this period, as he became involved in labor organizing and socialist advocacy.

In 1935, Cameron returned to Nova Scotia and took a position as a researcher for the Nova Scotia Department of Labour, where he worked until 1940. His research focused on unemployment, wages, and working conditions in the province’s coal and steel industries. During this time, he also became a prominent figure in the Cape Breton labor movement, serving as a negotiator for the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) and helping to secure better wages and safety standards for miners. His efforts contributed to the successful 1939 strike at the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation (DOSCO), which resulted in a 10% wage increase for workers.

Cameron’s political career began in 1941 when he was elected to the Nova Scotia House of Assembly as the CCF member for Cape Breton North. At 33, he was one of the youngest legislators in the province’s history. During his first term, he advocated for social welfare programs, public healthcare, and workers’ rights, often clashing with the conservative government of Premier Angus L. Macdonald. In 1945, he was re-elected, and his influence grew as the CCF gained support among industrial workers and farmers. That same year, he married Margaret MacDonald, a schoolteacher from Sydney, with whom he had three children: Alexander (born 1946), Mary (born 1948), and John (born 1951).

In 1949, Cameron made the transition to federal politics, winning a seat in the House of Commons as the CCF member for Cape Breton North and Victoria. He served in Parliament for 14 years, from 1949 to 1963, becoming one of the party’s most vocal advocates for universal healthcare, old-age pensions, and unemployment insurance. His most notable achievement came in 1957, when he played a key role in the passage of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, which laid the groundwork for Canada’s national healthcare system. As a member of the Joint Committee on Old Age Security, he also helped draft the Old Age Security Act of 1951, which established a universal pension for Canadians over 70.

Outside of politics, Cameron was a prolific writer and lecturer. He authored several books and pamphlets on labor issues, including *The Coal Miners of Nova Scotia* (1948) and *Socialism and the Canadian Worker* (1955). He also served as a visiting professor at Dalhousie University in Halifax from 1960 to 1962, teaching courses on labor economics. His academic work was widely cited in discussions about industrial relations and social policy.

Cameron retired from federal politics in 1963, choosing not to seek re-election. After leaving Parliament, he remained active in public life, serving as a labor arbitrator and consultant for the Nova Scotia government. He also continued to write, publishing his memoirs, *A Life in Politics*, in 1970. In his later years, he divided his time between Halifax and Sydney, where he was a frequent speaker at community events and labor gatherings.

Daniel Alexander Cameron died on March 12, 1985, at the age of 76, in Halifax, Nova Scotia. He was survived by his wife, Margaret, who passed away in 1998, and his three children. His legacy endures in Canada’s social welfare system, particularly in the establishment of universal healthcare, and in the labor movement, where he is remembered as a tireless advocate for workers’ rights. His papers are housed in the Beaton Institute at Cape Breton University, where they remain an important resource for historians studying 20th-century Canadian politics.

title: Shin Jea-hwan
text:
Shin Jea-hwan was born on August 3, 1994, in Seoul, South Korea. From a young age, he displayed a keen interest in music and performance, influenced by his family’s appreciation for the arts. His parents, though not professionally involved in entertainment, encouraged his creative pursuits. Shin attended Seoul Arts High School, a prestigious institution known for nurturing young talent in the performing arts, where he honed his vocal and dance skills. After graduating in 2013, he enrolled at Seoul Institute of the Arts, majoring in acting, further refining his craft in both singing and stage performance.

Shin’s professional career began in earnest when he joined the South Korean boy group *ROMEO* under Pony Canyon Korea. The group debuted on May 7, 2015, with the single "Lovesick," but despite their efforts, they struggled to gain significant traction in the competitive K-pop industry. *ROMEO* released several EPs, including *The ROMEO* (2015) and *Zero In* (2016), but commercial success remained elusive. The group eventually disbanded in 2017, leaving Shin to explore other opportunities.

Undeterred, Shin transitioned into musical theater, a field where his vocal training and stage presence could shine. His breakthrough came in 2018 when he was cast in the Korean production of *The Days*, a musical based on the life of former South Korean President Kim Dae-jung. His performance as the young Kim Dae-jung earned critical acclaim, showcasing his ability to convey deep emotion and complexity. That same year, he joined the cast of *Mozart!*, playing the lead role of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, a demanding part that required both vocal prowess and dramatic range. His portrayal was widely praised, solidifying his reputation as a rising star in musical theater.

In 2019, Shin auditioned for the reality survival show *Produce X 101*, which aired on Mnet from May to July. The program aimed to form a temporary boy group from 101 trainees, with the final lineup determined by audience votes. Shin initially struggled to stand out but gained momentum through his consistent performances and charismatic stage presence. In the finale on July 19, 2019, he finished in first place with 1,038,122 votes, securing a spot in the final group, *X1*. The group debuted on August 27, 2019, with the EP *Emergency: Quantum Leap*, which topped the Gaon Album Chart. However, *X1*’s career was short-lived due to controversies surrounding vote manipulation in *Produce X 101*. The group disbanded on January 6, 2020, after just five months.

Following the disbandment, Shin returned to musical theater, starring in *Werther* (2020) as the titular character, a role that further demonstrated his dramatic depth. He also participated in *Immortal Songs: Singing the Legend*, a popular South Korean music program, where he won an episode with his rendition of "The Flight" in 2021. His versatility as a performer was evident as he seamlessly transitioned between musical theater and television appearances.

In 2022, Shin made his solo debut with the digital single "Switch," released on March 14. The song showcased his vocal abilities and marked a new chapter in his career. Later that year, he joined the cast of *The Devil*, a musical adaptation of the Broadway hit *The Devil Wears Prada*, playing the role of Nigel Kipling. His performance earned him the Best Supporting Actor award at the 2023 Korean Musical Awards, a testament to his growth as an artist.

Beyond his professional achievements, Shin has maintained a relatively private personal life. He is known for his disciplined work ethic and dedication to his craft, often sharing behind-the-scenes insights with fans through social media. As of 2024, he continues to balance musical theater and solo music projects, with plans to expand his repertoire in both fields. His journey from a struggling idol trainee to an acclaimed musical theater actor and solo artist reflects his resilience and passion for performance.

title: Gemma Arterton
text:
Gemma Christina Arterton was born on January 12, 1986, in Gravesend, Kent, England. She was the first child of Sally-Anne Heap, a cleaner and amateur actress, and Barry Arterton, a welder. Her younger sister, Hannah Jane Arterton, was born in 1989 and later also pursued an acting career. Gemma was born with polydactyly, a condition that gave her an extra finger on each hand, which was surgically removed shortly after birth. Raised in a working-class family, she attended Gravesend Grammar School for Girls before receiving a scholarship to study at the Miskin Theatre at North West Kent College in Dartford. At the age of 16, she enrolled in the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London, graduating in 2007 with a Bachelor of Arts in Acting.

Arterton’s professional acting career began almost immediately after her graduation. Her first major role came in 2007 when she was cast as Kelly in the British television miniseries *Capturing Mary*, directed by Stephen Poliakoff. That same year, she made her feature film debut in the low-budget horror movie *St. Trinian’s*, playing the minor role of Head Girl. However, her breakthrough came in 2008 when she was selected from over 1,500 actresses to play the Bond Girl Strawberry Fields in *Quantum of Solace*, the 22nd James Bond film. The role, though small, earned her widespread recognition and a nomination for Best Newcomer at the 2008 Empire Awards.

Following her Bond debut, Arterton’s career accelerated rapidly. In 2009, she starred as the Greek goddess Io in *Clash of the Titans*, a fantasy film directed by Louis Leterrier, which grossed over $493 million worldwide. That same year, she played the lead role of Tamara Drewe in *Tamara Drewe*, a comedy-drama based on the graphic novel by Posy Simmonds. The film, released in 2010, was a commercial success and further established her as a leading actress in British cinema. For her performance, she received a nomination for the British Comedy Award for Best Comedy Actress.

Throughout the early 2010s, Arterton continued to take on diverse roles in both independent and mainstream films. In 2010, she starred in *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* as Princess Tamina, a role that earned her a Teen Choice Award nomination for Choice Movie Actress: Action. She also appeared in *The Disappearance of Alice Creed* (2009), a tense thriller where she played the kidnapped victim, showcasing her ability to handle more dramatic material. In 2012, she took on the role of the title character in *Byzantium*, a vampire film directed by Neil Jordan, and starred in *Song for Marion* (2012), a drama about a choir for the elderly, alongside Vanessa Redgrave and Terence Stamp.

Arterton’s stage career also flourished during this period. In 2015, she made her West End debut in *Made in Dagenham*, a musical based on the 1968 Ford sewing machinists strike, for which she received an Olivier Award nomination for Best Actress in a Musical. The following year, she starred in *Nell Gwynn*, a play about the 17th-century actress and mistress of King Charles II, earning critical acclaim and another Olivier Award nomination, this time for Best Actress in a Play.

Beyond acting, Arterton has been involved in various philanthropic efforts. In 2010, she became an ambassador for the UK charity Women for Women International, which supports women survivors of war. She has also been a vocal advocate for gender equality in the film industry, speaking out about the lack of opportunities for female directors and the gender pay gap. In 2016, she co-founded the production company Rebel Park Productions with her then-partner, actor Rory Keenan, aiming to develop projects with strong female leads.

In her personal life, Arterton has been married twice. Her first marriage was to Spanish fashion assistant Stefano Catelli in 2010, but the couple divorced in 2015. In 2019, she married Italian actor and director Rocco Fasano, with whom she has a son, born in 2023. Despite her success, Arterton has remained grounded, often speaking about her working-class roots and the challenges of navigating the entertainment industry.

In recent years, Arterton has continued to work in both film and theater. In 2019, she starred in *Summerland*, a World War II drama written and directed by Jessica Swale, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival. She also appeared in *The Escape* (2017), a drama about a woman seeking independence, and *Vita & Virginia* (2018), where she played writer Virginia Woolf. On stage, she returned to the West End in 2022 for *The Crucible*, playing Elizabeth Proctor opposite Brendan Gleeson.

As of 2024, Gemma Arterton remains one of the most versatile and respected actresses of her generation, with a career spanning film, television, and theater. Her ability to balance commercial success with critically acclaimed performances has solidified her place in British cinema, while her advocacy work continues to highlight important social issues.

title: Kajal Aggarwal
text:
Kajal Aggarwal was born on June 19, 1985, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India, into a Punjabi Hindu family. Her father, Vinay Aggarwal, worked as an entrepreneur, while her mother, Suman Aggarwal, was a confectioner. Kajal has a younger sister, Nisha Aggarwal, who also briefly pursued acting.
