The trust has since funded the construction of several madrasas and orphanages across Bangladesh, including the Darul Uloom Mamunul Islam in Dhaka, which opened in 2021 and now serves over 1,200 students. He also became a regular speaker at international Islamic conferences, particularly in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, where he advocated for global Muslim unity.

Mamunul’s personal life has been relatively private, though it is known that he married in 2015 and has two children. Despite his controversial public persona, he has maintained a reputation for personal piety and discipline, often emphasizing the importance of moral conduct in his speeches. As of 2024, he continues to serve as the secretary general of Islami Andolon Bangladesh and remains an active voice in the country’s religious and political discourse. His career reflects the complex interplay between religion, politics, and social activism in contemporary Bangladesh, making him one of the most influential—and divisive—figures in the nation’s recent history.

title: Umika Kawashima
text:
Umika Kawashima was born on March 3, 1994, in Tokyo, Japan. She grew up in a middle-class family in the Setagaya Ward, where her parents encouraged her early interest in the performing arts. From a young age, Kawashima displayed a natural talent for singing and acting, participating in local theater productions and school talent shows. At the age of 10, she joined a children’s theater group in Tokyo, where she honed her skills in both acting and vocal performance. Her parents, recognizing her potential, enrolled her in acting and voice lessons, which laid the foundation for her future career.

Kawashima’s professional career began in 2007 when she was just 13 years old. She made her debut as a member of the idol group *9nine*, which was formed under the talent agency LesPros Entertainment. The group consisted of five members, including Kawashima, and debuted on September 19, 2007, with the single *"Shine."* *9nine* quickly gained popularity, particularly among teenage audiences, and Kawashima’s role as the youngest member brought her significant attention. Over the next several years, the group released multiple singles and albums, including *"Hikari no Kage"* (2008) and *"Cross Over"* (2010), which charted on the Oricon Weekly Singles Chart, with some reaching the top 20.

In addition to her work with *9nine*, Kawashima pursued acting opportunities. In 2009, she made her television debut in the NHK drama *"Tsubasa,"* where she played a supporting role. This was followed by appearances in other TV dramas, such as *"Q10"* (2010) and *"Kaseifu no Mita"* (2011), which further established her as a versatile performer. Her breakthrough acting role came in 2012 when she starred in the live-action adaptation of the manga *"Kuroko’s Basketball"* as Riko Aida. The film, released on March 3, 2012, was a commercial success, grossing over ¥2.5 billion ($23 million) in Japan, and Kawashima’s performance was widely praised.

Kawashima’s career continued to flourish in the following years. In 2013, she starred in the horror film *"Ju-on: The Beginning of the End,"* a reboot of the popular *Ju-on* franchise, where she played the lead role of Yui Shono. The film was released on June 28, 2014, and became a box office hit, earning over ¥1.5 billion ($14 million). Her performance in the film demonstrated her ability to tackle more mature and intense roles, expanding her range as an actress. That same year, she also appeared in the drama *"Nobunaga Concerto,"* which aired on Fuji TV, further solidifying her reputation in the industry.

Despite her success, Kawashima faced challenges in balancing her music and acting careers. In 2015, *9nine* announced a hiatus, allowing its members to focus on individual projects. Kawashima took this opportunity to deepen her acting career, appearing in films such as *"The Big Bee"* (2015) and *"The Last Cop: The Movie"* (2017). She also returned to television, starring in the 2016 drama *"Love That Makes You Cry,"* which aired on Fuji TV and garnered high ratings.

In 2018, Kawashima made her stage debut in the musical *"Les Misérables,"* where she played the role of Cosette. The production ran from November 2018 to January 2019 at the Imperial Theatre in Tokyo, and her performance was well-received by critics and audiences alike. This role marked a significant milestone in her career, showcasing her versatility as a performer beyond film and television.

Kawashima’s personal life has remained relatively private, though she has occasionally shared insights into her interests and hobbies. She is known to be an avid reader and enjoys traveling, often documenting her trips on social media. In 2020, she announced her marriage to a non-celebrity partner, though she has kept details about her spouse and family life out of the public eye.

As of 2024, Kawashima continues to work in the entertainment industry, balancing acting roles with occasional music projects. She has expressed a desire to explore more diverse roles, including international productions, and remains a respected figure in Japanese pop culture. Her career, spanning over 15 years, reflects her dedication to her craft and her ability to adapt to the evolving demands of the entertainment industry.

title: Chris John (boxer)
text:
Chris John, born Yohannes Christian John on September 14, 1979, in Banjarnegara, Central Java, Indonesia, is one of the most successful boxers in Indonesian history. Raised in a modest family, John was introduced to boxing at a young age by his father, Johan Tjahjadi, a former amateur boxer who recognized his son’s potential. The family later moved to Jakarta, where John began training more seriously under the guidance of his father and local coaches. His early amateur career was promising, though unremarkable, as he compiled a record of 25 wins and 5 losses before turning professional in 1998 at the age of 18.

John made his professional debut on January 2, 1998, in Jakarta, defeating fellow Indonesian boxer Firman Kanda by a second-round technical knockout (TKO). Over the next two years, he built an undefeated record, winning 16 consecutive fights, 10 by knockout, and capturing the Indonesian featherweight title in 1999. His disciplined training regimen and technical precision quickly set him apart in the regional boxing scene. By 2001, he had moved up to the international stage, defeating Thai boxer Pongsaklek Wonjongkam by unanimous decision in Jakarta to claim the PABA (Pan Asian Boxing Association) featherweight title.

His breakthrough came on September 26, 2003, when he faced Oscar León of Colombia for the WBA featherweight interim title in Jakarta. John won the fight by unanimous decision, setting the stage for a full world title shot. On April 3, 2004, he challenged WBA featherweight champion Derrick Gainer of the United States in Jakarta. In a closely contested bout, John won by split decision, becoming Indonesia’s third world boxing champion after Ellyas Pical and Nico Thomas. He successfully defended the title a record 18 times over the next decade, a feat that cemented his legacy as one of the longest-reigning champions in the division’s history.

John’s reign as WBA featherweight champion was marked by a series of high-profile defenses against top contenders. Notable victories included a unanimous decision over Mexican boxer Juan Manuel Márquez on March 4, 2006, in Las Vegas—a fight that showcased his ability to compete on the global stage. He also defeated Roinet Caballero of Panama by unanimous decision on December 17, 2005, and later retained his title against Japanese boxer Hiroyuki Enoki on October 24, 2008, in a hard-fought bout in Tokyo. His most controversial defense came on February 28, 2009, against Venezuelan boxer Rocky Juarez in Houston, Texas, where many observers believed Juarez had done enough to win. The fight was ruled a split-decision draw, allowing John to retain his title.

Despite his dominance, John’s career was not without challenges. He struggled to secure fights against the division’s top pound-for-pound talents, such as Manny Pacquiao, due to promotional and political obstacles within the sport. His style, characterized by precise footwork, sharp counterpunching, and defensive mastery, made him a difficult opponent but also limited his mainstream appeal. On December 6, 2013, after nearly a decade as champion, John lost his title to South African boxer Simpiwe Vetyeka in Marina Bay Sands, Singapore. The fight was stopped in the sixth round due to a cut over John’s right eye, resulting in a technical decision victory for Vetyeka.

Following the loss, John announced his retirement from professional boxing on January 28, 2014, at the age of 34. His final record stood at 48 wins (22 knockouts), 1 loss, and 3 draws, with 18 successful title defenses. After retiring, John remained involved in boxing as a promoter and mentor to younger Indonesian fighters. He also ventured into business, opening a fitness center in Jakarta and investing in real estate. In recognition of his contributions to Indonesian sports, he received numerous awards, including the prestigious Satyalancana Kebudayaan (Cultural Merit Award) from the Indonesian government in 2014.

John’s personal life has been relatively private. He married his longtime girlfriend, Anna Maria, in 2005, and the couple has two children. Despite his fame, he has maintained a low-profile lifestyle, focusing on family and business ventures. His legacy in Indonesian boxing remains unmatched, as he is widely regarded as the country’s greatest professional boxer, surpassing even the achievements of his predecessors. In 2020, he was inducted into the Indonesian Boxing Hall of Fame, further solidifying his place in the nation’s sporting history.

title: Ki Fitzgerald
text:
Ki Fitzgerald, born Kathleen Irene Fitzgerald on March 12, 1923, in Chicago, Illinois, was an American actress and singer whose career spanned several decades, primarily during the mid-20th century. She grew up in a working-class Irish-American family in the South Side of Chicago, the youngest of five children born to James Fitzgerald, a police officer, and Margaret O’Donnell Fitzgerald, a homemaker. From an early age, Fitzgerald displayed a talent for performance, participating in school plays and local theater productions. She attended St. Mary’s High School, where she was an active member of the drama club, and later enrolled in the Goodman School of Drama at the Art Institute of Chicago, graduating in 1942.

Fitzgerald’s professional career began in earnest in the early 1940s, when she moved to New York City to pursue acting. She made her Broadway debut in the 1943 production of *Oklahoma!* as a member of the ensemble, though she did not have a speaking role. Her first credited stage appearance came in 1944 in the musical *Follow the Girls*, where she played the role of Mimi, a chorus girl. The show ran for 882 performances at the New Century Theatre, establishing Fitzgerald as a reliable performer in the competitive world of New York theater. During this period, she also appeared in several USO shows, entertaining troops during World War II alongside other rising stars like Gene Kelly and Mickey Rooney.

In 1947, Fitzgerald transitioned to film, signing a contract with Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM). Her first major screen role was in the 1948 musical *Easter Parade*, starring Fred Astaire and Judy Garland, where she played a featured dancer in the "Steppin’ Out with My Baby" number. Though her part was small, her performance caught the attention of critics and audiences alike. Over the next decade, she appeared in over a dozen films, including *Annie Get Your Gun* (1950), where she played Winnie Tate, one of Annie Oakley’s sisters, and *Show Boat* (1951), in which she had a supporting role as a chorus girl. Fitzgerald’s film career peaked in the early 1950s, with notable appearances in *Singin’ in the Rain* (1952), where she danced alongside Debbie Reynolds in the "Good Morning" sequence, and *The Band Wagon* (1953), starring Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse.

Despite her success in Hollywood, Fitzgerald remained deeply connected to the stage. In 1955, she returned to Broadway in the original production of *Damn Yankees*, playing the role of Gloria Thorpe, a seductive reporter. The show was a critical and commercial success, running for 1,019 performances at the 46th Street Theatre. Her performance earned her a Tony Award nomination for Best Featured Actress in a Musical in 1956, though she ultimately lost to Judy Holliday for *Bells Are Ringing*. Fitzgerald’s versatility as a performer was further demonstrated in 1959 when she starred in the national tour of *Gypsy*, playing the role of Louise, the younger sister of Gypsy Rose Lee.

By the 1960s, Fitzgerald’s career began to slow as the golden age of Hollywood musicals waned. She made her final film appearance in 1962’s *Billy Rose’s Jumbo*, a musical comedy starring Doris Day and Stephen Boyd. After this, she shifted her focus back to theater and television, appearing in guest roles on popular shows such as *The Ed Sullivan Show* (1963) and *The Red Skelton Show* (1964). In 1965, she married actor and director Robert Lewis, a co-founder of the Actors Studio, and the couple settled in New York City. Fitzgerald continued to perform in regional theater productions and dinner theaters throughout the 1970s and 1980s, including a 1978 revival of *Oklahoma!* at the Goodspeed Opera House in Connecticut.

In her later years, Fitzgerald dedicated much of her time to teaching. She became a respected acting coach, working with young performers at the HB Studio in New York City and the American Academy of Dramatic Arts. She also occasionally returned to the stage, including a 1992 appearance in a benefit performance of *Follies* at the Shubert Theatre in Boston. Fitzgerald remained active in the entertainment industry until her health began to decline in the early 2000s. She passed away on October 15, 2004, at the age of 81, in her Manhattan apartment, due to complications from pneumonia. She was survived by her husband, Robert Lewis, who died in 1997, and her sister, Margaret Fitzgerald O’Brien. Fitzgerald’s contributions to American theater and film, though sometimes overshadowed by her more famous contemporaries, remain a testament to her talent and dedication as a performer.

title: Tom Coburn
text:
Thomas Allen Coburn was born on March 14, 1948, in Casper, Wyoming, to Orin Wesley Coburn and Anita Joy Allen Coburn. His family later moved to Muskogee, Oklahoma, where he spent most of his formative years. Coburn attended Muskogee Central High School, graduating in 1966. He then enrolled at Oklahoma State University, earning a Bachelor of Science degree in accounting in 1970. After completing his undergraduate studies, Coburn pursued a medical degree at the University of Oklahoma College of Medicine, graduating in 1983. During his time in medical school, he also earned a Master of Business Administration from the University of Oklahoma in 1981.

Coburn began his medical career as a family physician, opening a private practice in Muskogee in 1983. He gained a reputation for his dedication to patient care, often treating low-income and uninsured individuals. His medical practice became well-known in the community, and he delivered over 4,000 babies during his career as a physician. Coburn’s work in medicine was marked by a commitment to conservative principles, including limited government intervention in healthcare.

In 1994, Coburn entered politics, running for Oklahoma’s 2nd Congressional District seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. He won the election, defeating Democrat Virgil Cooper with 52% of the vote. Coburn served in the House from January 3, 1995, to January 3, 2001, during which time he became known for his fiscal conservatism and opposition to government waste. He was a key figure in the Republican freshman class of 1994, which helped secure a GOP majority in the House for the first time in 40 years. Coburn co-authored the *Citizens Against Government Waste’s Congressional Pig Book*, which highlighted pork-barrel spending, and he famously pledged to serve no more than three terms, honoring that commitment by not seeking re-election in 2000.

After leaving Congress, Coburn returned to his medical practice but remained active in public policy. In 2004, he ran for the U.S. Senate, winning the Republican primary and defeating Democrat Brad Carson in the general election with 53% of the vote. He served in the Senate from January 3, 2005, to January 3, 2015. During his tenure, Coburn earned a reputation as a fierce fiscal watchdog, often clashing with members of both parties over government spending. He was a leading voice in opposition to earmarks and wasteful expenditures, famously blocking numerous bills he deemed fiscally irresponsible. One of his most notable actions was his use of Senate holds to delay or prevent legislation, including a 2007 attempt to block a $23 billion water projects bill that he argued contained excessive pork-barrel spending.

Coburn was also a vocal critic of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), commonly known as Obamacare, and played a key role in the 2013 government shutdown over funding for the law. Despite his hardline stance, he maintained a reputation for integrity and bipartisanship on certain issues. He worked with Senator Barack Obama on the *Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006*, which created a public database to track federal spending. Coburn also co-sponsored the *Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge (STOCK) Act* in 2012, which prohibited insider trading by members of Congress.

In 2014, Coburn announced his intention to resign from the Senate before the end of his term due to a recurrence of prostate cancer, which he had first been diagnosed with in 1996. He officially left office on January 3, 2015, and was succeeded by James Lankford, who won a special election to fill the remainder of his term. After his retirement, Coburn remained active in conservative policy circles, serving as a senior advisor to the Manhattan Institute and writing opinion pieces on fiscal responsibility.

Coburn’s later years were marked by a continued battle with cancer. He passed away on March 28, 2020, at the age of 72, in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Throughout his life, Coburn was known for his unwavering commitment to limited government, fiscal restraint, and personal integrity. His legacy includes significant contributions to government transparency and opposition to wasteful spending, leaving a lasting impact on both Oklahoma and national politics.

title: Chris Cuomo
text:
Christopher Charles Cuomo, known professionally as Chris Cuomo, was born on August 9, 1970, in Queens, New York City, to Mario Cuomo, a prominent Democratic politician who served as Governor of New York from 1983 to 1994, and Matilda Raffa Cuomo, an advocate for women’s and children’s rights. He is the youngest of five children, including his older brother Andrew Cuomo, who later became Governor of New York (2011–2021), and sister Maria Cuomo Cole, a documentary filmmaker. The family moved to Albany, New York, in 1983 when Mario Cuomo became governor, and Chris attended Albany Academy, a private preparatory school, graduating in 1988.

Cuomo earned his undergraduate degree from Yale University in 1993, where he studied political science. He later attended Fordham University School of Law in the Bronx, graduating with a Juris Doctor degree in 1995. Though he passed the New York State bar exam, Cuomo never practiced law, instead pivoting to journalism, a field that aligned more closely with his family’s public profile and his own interests.

Cuomo began his journalism career in 1995 as a reporter for CNBC, covering business and financial news. His early work included segments on the stock market and corporate developments, but he quickly transitioned to more general news reporting. In 1999, he joined ABC News as a correspondent, where he covered major stories such as the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. His reporting from Ground Zero in the immediate aftermath of the attacks earned him recognition for his on-the-ground coverage. During his time at ABC, he also contributed to programs like *Good Morning America* and *20/20*, often focusing on legal and investigative stories.

In 2006, Cuomo became co-anchor of *Good Morning America*’s weekend edition alongside Kate Snow, a role he held until 2009. That same year, he launched *20/20*’s *Primetime* spin-off, *Primetime: What Would You Do?*, a hidden-camera show that explored ethical dilemmas and human behavior. The program ran for six seasons, from 2009 to 2015, and became one of ABC’s most popular newsmagazines, earning Cuomo a loyal following. During this period, he also covered high-profile trials, including the Casey Anthony and Jodi Arias cases, and reported from conflict zones such as Haiti after the 2010 earthquake.

Cuomo’s career reached a new height in 2013 when he joined CNN as anchor of *New Day*, the network’s morning news program, alongside co-anchor Kate Bolduan. The show premiered on June 17, 2013, and quickly became a key part of CNN’s lineup, competing with *Fox & Friends* and *Morning Joe*. Cuomo’s interviewing style—direct, sometimes confrontational, and deeply researched—set him apart in cable news. He covered major stories, including the 2016 presidential election, the Flint water crisis, and the Parkland school shooting in 2018. His interviews with figures like former FBI Director James Comey and White House advisor Kellyanne Conway drew significant attention, often generating headlines and viral moments.

In 2018, Cuomo launched *Cuomo Prime Time*, a weeknight primetime show on CNN that debuted on June 4. The program focused on political analysis, interviews, and investigative reporting, further cementing his role as one of the network’s most visible personalities. His brother Andrew’s governorship during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 brought Chris into the spotlight in a different way, as he frequently interviewed his brother on-air about New York’s response to the crisis. This dynamic drew criticism, with some accusing Chris of a conflict of interest, though he defended the interviews as newsworthy and transparent.

Cuomo’s career at CNN came to an abrupt end in December 2021 following revelations that he had advised his brother Andrew during the latter’s sexual harassment scandal, which ultimately led to Andrew’s resignation as governor in August 2021. An internal investigation found that Chris had used his media connections to gather information about his brother’s accusers, violating journalistic ethics. CNN suspended him on November 30, 2021, and terminated his employment on December 4, citing a breach of trust. The scandal overshadowed his professional achievements, including multiple Emmy nominations and a 2016 award for his coverage of the Flint water crisis.

After leaving CNN, Cuomo launched *The Chris Cuomo Project*, a Substack newsletter and podcast, in early 2022. The platform allowed him to continue offering political commentary and interviews, though it struggled to regain the audience he had at CNN. He also made occasional appearances on other networks, including NewsNation, where he hosted a short-lived prime-time show in 2023. Despite the controversy, Cuomo remained a polarizing but influential figure in media, known for his sharp interviewing skills and deep knowledge of politics and law.

Cuomo married Cristina Greeven in 2001, and the couple has three children: Bella, Mario, and Carolina. They reside in Manhattan. Outside of journalism, Cuomo has been involved in philanthropy, supporting organizations like the Bowery Mission and the Robin Hood Foundation, which combat poverty in New York City. His career, marked by both professional success and personal controversy, reflects the complexities of modern media, where journalistic integrity and personal relationships often intersect in challenging ways.

title: David Oyite-Ojok
text:
David Oyite-Ojok was born on January 15, 1940, in the village of Loro, located in present-day Oyam District in northern Uganda. He was the son of Ojok Loro, a local chief, and grew up in a region that was then part of the Lango District under British colonial rule. His early education began at Loro Primary School before he moved to Boroboro Junior Secondary School and later attended Gulu High School, where he completed his secondary education in 1959. Oyite-Ojok was known for his discipline and leadership qualities from a young age, traits that would later define his military career.

After finishing school, Oyite-Ojok joined the Uganda Police Force in 1960 as a cadet. He underwent training at the Police Training School in Kampala and was commissioned as an Assistant Superintendent of Police in 1962, the year Uganda gained independence from Britain. His early police career was marked by postings in various parts of the country, including Jinja and Mbale, where he gained experience in maintaining law and order. However, his ambitions soon led him to transition into the military. In 1964, he joined the Uganda Army as a Second Lieutenant after completing a six-month officer training course at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in the United Kingdom.

Oyite-Ojok’s military career advanced rapidly. By 1966, he had been promoted to Captain and was serving under Prime Minister Milton Obote during a politically turbulent period. That same year, Obote suspended the constitution, declared himself president, and abolished the traditional kingdoms, including Buganda, leading to a violent confrontation with the Kabaka (King) of Buganda. Oyite-Ojok played a key role in the military operation that stormed the Kabaka’s palace at Mengo, forcing the Kabaka into exile. His loyalty to Obote earned him further promotions, and by 1968, he was a Major and commander of the 1st Battalion in Jinja.

In 1971, Idi Amin staged a military coup while Obote was attending a Commonwealth summit in Singapore. Oyite-Ojok, who was then a Lieutenant Colonel and commander of the Malire Mechanized Regiment, was among the officers who resisted the coup. After its success, he fled into exile in Tanzania, where he joined other Obote loyalists in planning a counter-coup. Over the next eight years, he became a central figure in the Uganda National Liberation Army (UNLA), a rebel group formed with Tanzanian support to overthrow Amin. In 1979, the combined forces of the UNLA and the Tanzanian People’s Defence Force (TPDF) invaded Uganda, leading to Amin’s downfall in April of that year. Oyite-Ojok played a crucial role in the military campaign, particularly in the battles around Kampala and Jinja.

Following Amin’s ouster, Oyite-Ojok was appointed Chief of Staff of the UNLA in June 1979, with the rank of Brigadier. He was instrumental in restructuring the army and maintaining stability during the interim government led by Yusuf Lule and later Godfrey Binaisa. When Obote returned to power in the disputed December 1980 elections, Oyite-Ojok was promoted to Major General and confirmed as Chief of Staff. His leadership was critical in the early years of Obote’s second presidency, as the government faced a growing insurgency led by Yoweri Museveni’s National Resistance Army (NRA).

Oyite-Ojok’s military strategy focused on counterinsurgency operations in the Luweero Triangle, where the NRA was gaining strength. He commanded large-scale offensives, including Operation Bonanza in 1981, which aimed to crush rebel forces but also resulted in widespread civilian casualties. Despite his efforts, the war dragged on, and the UNLA struggled with discipline and morale. By 1983, Oyite-Ojok had become one of the most powerful figures in Uganda, overseeing a military that had grown to over 20,000 soldiers.

On December 2, 1983, Oyite-Ojok died in a helicopter crash near the town of Kiboga, under circumstances that remain disputed. The official explanation was that the helicopter, a Soviet-made Mi-8, malfunctioned due to mechanical failure. However, some accounts suggest sabotage, possibly linked to internal power struggles within the Obote government. His death was a significant blow to the UNLA and Obote’s regime, which ultimately collapsed in 1985. Oyite-Ojok was buried in his home village of Loro with full military honors. He was survived by his wife, Margaret Oyite-Ojok, and several children. His legacy remains contentious, with some viewing him as a loyal soldier who defended Uganda’s constitutional order, while others criticize his role in the brutal counterinsurgency campaigns of the early 1980s.

title: Thomas Piketty
text:
Thomas Piketty was born on May 7, 1971, in Clichy, a suburb of Paris, France. His parents were politically engaged, with his father involved in the Trotskyist movement before shifting to ecological activism. Piketty grew up in a left-leaning intellectual environment, which later influenced his academic and political views. He attended the Lycée Louis-le-Grand, one of France’s most prestigious secondary schools, where he excelled in mathematics and economics. In 1989, at the age of 18, he entered the École Normale Supérieure (ENS), a elite French grande école, where he studied mathematics and economics.

After completing his undergraduate studies at ENS in 1993, Piketty moved to the United States to pursue a Ph.D. in economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His doctoral thesis, completed in 1993 under the supervision of economist Peter Diamond, focused on wealth redistribution. The dissertation, titled *"Essays on the Theory of Redistribution and Taxation,"* explored how fiscal policies could address economic inequality. During his time at MIT, he also worked with economist Emmanuel Saez, who would later become a frequent collaborator.

Piketty returned to France in 1995 and began his academic career at the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales (EHESS) and the Paris School of Economics, where he became a professor. His early research focused on income and wealth distribution, particularly in historical and comparative perspectives. In 2001, he published *"Les Hauts Revenus en France au 20e Siècle"* (*"High Incomes in France in the 20th Century"*), a groundbreaking study that analyzed tax records to track income inequality in France over the past century. The book demonstrated how inequality had declined during the mid-20th century but began rising again in the 1980s.

Piketty’s most influential work, *"Capital in the Twenty-First Century,"* was published in French in 2013 (*"Le Capital au XXIe Siècle"*) and in English in 2014. The book, which drew on centuries of economic data from over 20 countries, argued that wealth inequality tends to increase when the rate of return on capital (r) exceeds the rate of economic growth (g), a phenomenon he summarized as r > g. The book became an international bestseller, selling over 2.5 million copies worldwide and sparking widespread debate about capitalism, taxation, and inequality. It was praised for its empirical rigor but also criticized by some economists for its policy prescriptions, such as a global wealth tax.

Beyond his academic work, Piketty has been actively involved in public policy debates. In 2007, he co-founded the Paris School of Economics, where he served as the first director until 2015. He has also advised political figures, including French Socialist Party leader François Hollande during his 2012 presidential campaign. However, Piketty later criticized Hollande’s economic policies, particularly the lack of progressive taxation. In 2015, he published *"The Economics of Inequality,"* a shorter, more accessible book that summarized his research on income and wealth disparities.

In 2019, Piketty released *"Capital and Ideology,"* a follow-up to his earlier work that expanded his analysis to include the historical and ideological justifications for inequality. The book examined how political and social structures have shaped economic disparities across different societies and eras. It was well-received but also faced criticism for its broad historical scope and some methodological choices.

Piketty has received numerous awards for his work, including the 2014 Yrjö Jahnsson Award, given by the European Economic Association to economists under 45 who have made significant contributions to the field. He has also been named one of the world’s most influential thinkers by *Foreign Policy* and *Prospect* magazines. Despite his global recognition, he remains based in France, where he continues to teach and research at the Paris School of Economics.

In his later years, Piketty has become more politically engaged, advocating for progressive taxation, wealth redistribution, and stronger labor protections. He has been a vocal critic of neoliberal economic policies and has called for a more egalitarian economic system. His work continues to shape debates on inequality, and he remains one of the most cited economists in the world. As of 2024, he is 53 years old and shows no signs of slowing down, with ongoing research projects and public engagements.

title: Richard Kuklinski
text:
Richard Leonard Kuklinski was born on April 11, 1935, in Jersey City, New Jersey, to a working-class Polish-American family. His father, Stanley Kuklinski, was a violent alcoholic who frequently beat his wife and children, while his mother, Anna McNally, was a devoutly religious woman who worked in a meatpacking plant. Kuklinski was the second of four children, and his turbulent upbringing was marked by extreme abuse. At the age of five, he witnessed his father beat his older brother, Florian, so severely that the boy died from his injuries. Stanley Kuklinski was never charged, and the death was ruled an accident.

Kuklinski’s violent tendencies emerged early. As a teenager, he tortured and killed neighborhood cats and dogs, often freezing them to death as an experiment. By his late teens, he had already committed his first human murders. In 1949, at the age of 14, he claimed to have beaten a local bully to death with a metal pipe, though this was never officially confirmed. His criminal career began in earnest in the 1950s when he became involved in petty theft and armed robbery. By 1954, he was arrested for assault after a bar fight in Paterson, New Jersey, but served only a short sentence.

In the early 1960s, Kuklinski began working as a freelance hitman, offering his services to organized crime figures in New York and New Jersey. His first confirmed contract killing occurred in 1963 when he murdered a man named Gary Smith, a small-time criminal who had crossed the Gambino crime family. Kuklinski shot Smith in the head and disposed of the body in a drum of acid, a method he would later refine. Over the next three decades, he claimed to have killed between 100 and 250 people, though law enforcement estimates place the number closer to 30–50. His victims included rival gangsters, business associates, and even innocent bystanders who had angered him.

Kuklinski’s reputation grew due to his cold efficiency and willingness to use extreme violence. He was known to employ a variety of methods, including poisoning, strangulation, and firearms, but he favored cyanide because it left no trace. He also experimented with freezing bodies to obscure the time of death. One of his most notorious killings was that of Roy DeMeo, a Gambino family associate, in 1983. Kuklinski shot DeMeo in his car and left the body in the trunk, though the murder was never officially linked to him at the time. He also claimed to have killed Paul Hoffman, a corrupt New Jersey police officer, in 1973, though this was never proven.

Despite his criminal success, Kuklinski maintained a façade of normalcy. In 1961, he married Barbara Pedrici, a woman he met at a diner in Paterson. The couple had three children—Dwayne, Merrick, and Christin—and lived in Dumont, New Jersey. Kuklinski worked legitimate jobs, including as a film processing technician at a photo lab, to cover his illicit activities. His wife and children were unaware of his double life until his arrest.

Kuklinski’s downfall began in 1986 when an undercover operation by the New Jersey State Police and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms (ATF) targeted him. Posing as a hitman, ATF agent Dominick Polifrone recorded Kuklinski discussing murders and planning new hits. On December 17, 1986, Kuklinski was arrested in a sting operation at a diner in Paterson. He was charged with five murders, including those of Gary Smith, Daniel Deppner, and Louis Masgay. In 1988, he was convicted and sentenced to two consecutive life terms plus 30 years in prison.

While incarcerated, Kuklinski gave multiple interviews, including to HBO documentarians in the early 2000s, where he detailed his crimes with chilling detachment. He claimed to have worked for the Gambino, DeCavalcante, and Lucchese crime families, though some of his stories were later disputed. Kuklinski suffered from health problems in his later years, including heart disease and suspected dementia. On March 5, 2006, at the age of 70, he died of natural causes at St. Francis Medical Center in Trenton, New Jersey. His body was cremated, and his ashes were scattered in an undisclosed location. Despite his infamy, Kuklinski’s legacy remains one of the most disturbing examples of a contract killer operating within the American underworld.

title: Rangi Te Kanawa
text:
Rangi Te Kanawa, a distinguished New Zealand textile conservator and weaver of Māori descent, was born on 15 August 1951 in Wellington, New Zealand. She is of Ngāti Maniapoto and Te Āti Awa descent, two iwi (tribes) with deep cultural significance in the central North Island and Taranaki regions. Her parents, Kahu Te Kanawa and Te Rina Keenan, were both prominent figures in Māori arts and culture. Her father, Kahu, was a respected carver and weaver, while her mother, Te Rina, was a skilled weaver who played a crucial role in reviving traditional Māori textile techniques. This rich cultural heritage deeply influenced Rangi’s life and career.

Te Kanawa grew up in a household where Māori language, customs, and arts were central. She attended Wellington High School, where she developed an early interest in textiles and conservation. After completing her secondary education in 1969, she pursued further studies at the Wellington Polytechnic (now part of Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington), where she trained in textile conservation. Her formal education in this field was groundbreaking, as she became one of the first Māori women to specialise in the preservation of traditional Māori textiles, particularly *kākahu* (cloaks) and *whāriki* (woven mats).

In 1975, Te Kanawa began her career at the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa (then known as the National Museum of New Zealand) in Wellington. She started as a textile conservator, working on the preservation of the museum’s extensive collection of Māori and Pacific textiles. Her expertise quickly became invaluable, particularly in the care of fragile *kākahu*, some of which dated back to the 18th and 19th centuries. Over the next four decades, she played a pivotal role in developing conservation techniques tailored to Māori textiles, which often required different approaches from Western methods due to the use of natural fibres like *harakeke* (New Zealand flax), *muka* (processed flax fibre), and feathers.

One of Te Kanawa’s most significant contributions was her work on the conservation of the *Kahu Kiwi*, a rare and historically important cloak made from kiwi feathers, which had deteriorated significantly over time. Between 1990 and 1995, she led a meticulous restoration project, employing traditional weaving techniques alongside modern conservation practices. This project not only preserved the cloak but also provided new insights into the materials and methods used by Māori weavers in the past. Her work on this and other textiles earned her international recognition, including invitations to present at conferences in Australia, the United States, and Europe.

Beyond her conservation work, Te Kanawa was deeply committed to passing on her knowledge to future generations. From the 1980s onwards, she conducted numerous workshops and training programmes for Māori weavers and conservators, both in New Zealand and abroad. In 1998, she co-authored the book *Whatu Kākahu: Māori Cloaks*, a comprehensive study of Māori weaving techniques, which remains a key reference in the field. She also collaborated with institutions such as the Auckland War Memorial Museum and the British Museum, where she advised on the care of Māori textiles in their collections.

Te Kanawa’s achievements were formally recognised in 2002 when she was appointed a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit (MNZM) for her services to Māori arts and textile conservation. In 2018, she received an honorary Doctorate of Literature from Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington, acknowledging her lifetime of work in preserving and promoting Māori cultural heritage.

In her later years, Te Kanawa remained active in the field, serving as a mentor and advisor to emerging conservators and weavers. She continued to work with Te Papa, contributing to exhibitions such as *Kahu Ora: Living Cloaks* (2012–2013), which showcased the cultural and spiritual significance of Māori cloaks. Even after retiring from full-time work in 2015, she remained a respected figure in the Māori arts community, often consulted on matters of textile conservation and traditional weaving practices.

Rangi Te Kanawa passed away on 12 March 2023 in Wellington at the age of 71. Her legacy endures through the countless textiles she helped preserve, the knowledge she shared with others, and the generations of weavers and conservators she inspired. Her life’s work ensured that the art of Māori weaving would continue to thrive, bridging the past and the future.

title: Mohamed Abdi Mohamed
text:
Mohamed Abdi Mohamed, commonly known as Mohamed Abdi "Gandhi," was a prominent Somali politician, academic, and diplomat born on January 1, 1951, in the town of Belet Weyne, situated in the Hiran region of central Somalia. His early life was shaped by the post-colonial era, as Somalia gained independence from Italy and Britain in 1960. He hailed from the Hawadle sub-clan of the larger Hawiye clan, one of Somalia’s major ethnic groups. His father, Abdi Mohamed, was a local merchant, and his mother, Amina Hassan, was a homemaker, providing him with a modest but stable upbringing.

Gandhi received his primary and secondary education in Belet Weyne before moving to Mogadishu, Somalia’s capital, to pursue higher studies. In 1970, he enrolled at the Somali National University, where he earned a Bachelor’s degree in Political Science in 1974. His academic prowess and political awareness led him to further his education abroad. In 1976, he traveled to Italy, where he obtained a Master’s degree in International Relations from the University of Rome La Sapienza in 1978. His thesis focused on post-colonial African governance, reflecting his early interest in political systems and diplomacy.

Upon returning to Somalia in 1979, Gandhi joined the Somali Ministry of Foreign Affairs as a junior diplomat. His first significant posting was in 1980, when he served as a political officer at the Somali Embassy in Rome, Italy, a role he held until 1983. During this period, he gained valuable experience in international diplomacy, particularly in navigating Somalia’s relations with European nations amid the Cold War tensions. In 1984, he was transferred to the Somali Embassy in Washington, D.C., where he worked as a counselor until 1987. His tenure in the U.S. coincided with Somalia’s strategic alignment with the West, particularly the United States, during the Ogaden War with Ethiopia.

Gandhi’s political career took a more prominent turn in the late 1980s. In 1988, he was appointed as the Somali Ambassador to Kenya, a critical posting given the strained relations between the two countries over border disputes and Somalia’s support for ethnic Somali rebels in Kenya’s North Eastern Province. He played a key role in mediating tensions, though his efforts were often overshadowed by the escalating civil war in Somalia. He remained in Nairobi until 1990, when the collapse of Siad Barre’s regime forced him to return to Mogadishu.

With the outbreak of the Somali Civil War in 1991, Gandhi’s diplomatic career was disrupted, and he shifted his focus to academia and political activism. Between 1992 and 1995, he worked as a lecturer at the Somali National University, teaching courses on international relations and political theory. He also became involved in peacebuilding efforts, participating in numerous conferences aimed at reconciling Somalia’s warring factions. In 1996, he co-founded the Somali Institute for Peace and Human Rights, a non-governmental organization dedicated to conflict resolution and human rights advocacy.

Gandhi’s political career resumed in the early 2000s as Somalia began to show signs of stabilization. In 2004, he was appointed as the Minister of Planning and International Cooperation in the Transitional Federal Government (TFG), a position he held until 2007. During his tenure, he played a crucial role in securing international aid and coordinating reconstruction efforts. Notably, he helped negotiate a $21 million grant from the World Bank in 2006 to fund infrastructure projects in Mogadishu and other key regions. In 2008, he was appointed as the Minister of Defense, where he focused on rebuilding the Somali National Army and combating the growing threat of Al-Shabaab, the Islamist militant group.

One of Gandhi’s most significant achievements came in 2010 when he was elected as the President of the Interim Juba Administration, a regional government established in southern Somalia under the TFG’s federal framework. He served in this role until 2013, overseeing the administration of the Juba regions, including Kismayo, a strategically important port city. His leadership was marked by efforts to restore stability, improve local governance, and foster economic development. Under his administration, Kismayo’s port was reopened in 2012, generating an estimated $2 million in monthly revenue for the regional government.

In his later years, Gandhi remained active in Somali politics, though his influence waned as new leaders emerged. He served as a senior advisor to the Federal Government of Somalia from 2014 to 2016, contributing to policy discussions on federalism and security. In 2017, he retired from active politics but continued to engage in public discourse through occasional lectures and opinion pieces. He also became a vocal advocate for Somali unity and reconciliation, often criticizing clan-based divisions that had fueled decades of conflict.

Mohamed Abdi Mohamed passed away on March 15, 2021, in Nairobi, Kenya, at the age of 70. The cause of death was complications from a long-term illness. His funeral was held in Mogadishu, where he was buried with full state honors. He is survived by his wife, Fadumo Ali, and their five children. Throughout his career, Gandhi was widely respected for his diplomatic skills, academic contributions, and commitment to peacebuilding in Somalia. His legacy endures in the institutions he helped build and the policies he championed during a tumultuous period in Somali history.

title: Adnan Sami
text:
Adnan Sami was born on August 15, 1971, in London, England, to Arshad Sami Khan, a Pakistani diplomat and former Air Force officer, and Naureen Khan, a British woman of Indian descent. His family background was culturally rich, with roots in both South Asia and the West. Sami spent his early childhood in the United Kingdom before moving to Pakistan at the age of six when his father was posted there. He grew up in Islamabad, where he attended the prestigious Islamabad College for Boys. From a young age, Sami displayed an extraordinary aptitude for music, learning to play the piano at the age of five. By the time he was nine, he had already composed his first piece of music, a feat that hinted at his future career.

Sami’s formal education took him to the United Kingdom, where he enrolled at the Rugby School in Warwickshire at the age of 16. He later studied law and economics at King’s College London, graduating in 1991. However, his passion for music remained undiminished, and he soon shifted his focus entirely to a career in the arts. In 1989, at the age of 18, Sami released his first album, *The One & Only*, under the EMI label. The album featured a mix of Western pop and classical music, showcasing his virtuosity on the piano. His second album, *Raag Time*, released in 1991, blended Indian classical music with Western styles, earning him critical acclaim in both Pakistan and India.

Sami’s breakthrough in India came in the mid-1990s when he collaborated with Indian musicians and composers. In 1994, he composed and performed the song "Bheegi Bheegi Raat" for the Bollywood film *Sajan*, which became a hit. His work on the soundtrack of *Akele Hum Akele Tum* (1995) further cemented his reputation as a versatile musician. By the late 1990s, Sami had established himself as a prominent figure in the Indian music industry, known for his ability to fuse Eastern and Western musical traditions. In 1999, he released *Kabhi To Nazar Milao*, an album that included the title track, which became one of his most popular songs in India. The album sold over 500,000 copies, a significant achievement for an artist at the time.

In 2000, Sami made the decision to move to Mumbai, India, to pursue his career more actively in Bollywood. His move was met with success, as he composed and performed for several high-profile films, including *Dil Ka Rishta* (2003) and *Lucky: No Time for Love* (2005). His song "Lift Kara De" from *Lucky* became a chart-topper and remains one of his most recognizable tracks. Sami’s contributions to Indian cinema earned him numerous awards, including the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director in 2003 for *Saathiya*. He was also recognized for his live performances, often selling out venues across India and internationally. In 2005, he performed at the Royal Albert Hall in London, becoming one of the few South Asian artists to achieve this milestone.

Beyond music, Sami ventured into television as a judge on reality shows like *Sa Re Ga Ma Pa L’il Champs* (2006) and *India’s Got Talent* (2009–2011). His expertise and charismatic personality made him a popular figure on Indian television. In 2015, Sami became a naturalized citizen of India, a decision that reflected his deep connection to the country where he had built his career. The following year, he released his first single as an Indian citizen, "Bhar Do Jholi Meri," which was well-received.

Sami’s personal life has seen its share of challenges. He married his first wife, actress Zeba Bakhtiar, in 1993, but the marriage ended in divorce in 1997. He later married Dubai-based Arab Sabina in 2001, with whom he had two children, Azaan and Medina. However, this marriage also ended in divorce in 2010. In 2010, Sami faced a highly publicized legal battle with his second wife over custody of their children, which was resolved in his favor in 2011. Despite these personal struggles, Sami continued to focus on his music and career.

In 2018, Sami released the song "Main Hoon Saath Tere," which became a viral sensation and garnered millions of views on YouTube. His ability to reinvent himself and stay relevant in the ever-changing music industry has been a hallmark of his career. By 2020, Sami had released over 20 albums and composed music for more than 50 films. He has also been recognized with several honors, including the Padma Shri, India’s fourth-highest civilian award, in 2020, for his contributions to the arts.

In his later years, Sami has continued to perform and record music, maintaining a strong presence in both live concerts and digital platforms. His health has been a topic of public concern, particularly after he revealed in 2016 that he had lost over 130 kilograms (287 pounds) following a life-threatening weight condition. His transformation was widely covered in the media, and he has since become an advocate for healthy living. As of 2024, Adnan Sami remains an active and influential figure in the music industry, celebrated for his talent, resilience, and contributions to both Indian and international music.

title: Pallavi Joshi
text:
Pallavi Joshi was born on April 4, 1969, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India, into a family with a strong cultural and artistic background. Her father, Dilip Joshi, was a noted Marathi writer and journalist, while her mother, Usha Joshi, was a homemaker. Growing up in a household that valued literature and the arts, Pallavi developed an early interest in acting and performance. She attended St. Xavier’s College in Mumbai, where she pursued a degree in psychology, but her passion for acting soon led her to explore opportunities in the entertainment industry.

Pallavi Joshi began her acting career as a child artist in the late 1970s. One of her earliest notable roles was in the 1979 Hindi film *Dada*, directed by Jugal Kishore. She gained wider recognition in 1986 with her performance in the National Award-winning film *Tamas*, a television miniseries directed by Govind Nihalani. The series, based on Bhisham Sahni’s novel of the same name, depicted the horrors of Partition and earned critical acclaim. Pallavi’s portrayal of a young girl caught in the violence of the era showcased her acting depth and established her as a serious talent in Indian cinema.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, Pallavi Joshi appeared in several Hindi and Marathi films, including *Andha Yudh* (1987), *Sardar* (1993), and *Woh Chokri* (1994). Her role in *Woh Chokri*, directed by Subhash Ghai, earned her the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actress in 1995. The film, which explored themes of child labor and exploitation, highlighted her ability to portray complex emotional characters. She also worked in television during this period, appearing in popular shows like *Mr. Yogi* (1989) and *Talaash* (1992).

Beyond acting, Pallavi Joshi ventured into filmmaking and production. In 2001, she co-founded the production company *Vishwa Mohan Pictures* with her husband, Vivek Agnihotri, a filmmaker and author. The company produced several films, including *Chocolate: Deep Dark Secrets* (2005) and *The Kashmir Files* (2022). *The Kashmir Files*, directed by Agnihotri, became one of the most controversial and commercially successful films of 2022, sparking nationwide debates about its portrayal of the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits in the 1990s. Pallavi played a key role in the film’s production and promotion, and her involvement drew both praise and criticism.

Pallavi Joshi’s contributions to Indian cinema and television have been recognized with several awards. In addition to her National Film Award for *Woh Chokri*, she received the Maharashtra State Film Award for Best Actress in 1996 for her role in the Marathi film *Kairee*. Her work in *Tamas* also earned her widespread acclaim, including a nomination for the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actress. Over the years, she has been associated with socially relevant projects, often choosing roles that address pressing issues such as gender inequality, communal violence, and political corruption.

In her personal life, Pallavi Joshi married Vivek Agnihotri in 1997. The couple has two children, a son named Shikhar Agnihotri and a daughter named Akshita Agnihotri. Despite her busy career, Pallavi has maintained a relatively private personal life, focusing on her family and professional commitments. She has also been involved in various social and cultural initiatives, including efforts to promote Indian classical music and theater.

In recent years, Pallavi Joshi has continued to work in both acting and production. She appeared in the 2019 film *The Tashkent Files*, another project directed by her husband, which explored the mysterious death of former Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri. The film was well-received for its investigative approach and earned her praise for her performance. She also served as a producer on the film, further cementing her role in the Indian film industry as a multifaceted talent.

Pallavi Joshi’s career spans over four decades, during which she has transitioned from a child artist to a respected actor, producer, and filmmaker. Her work has often reflected a commitment to storytelling that challenges societal norms and highlights historical injustices. Whether through her performances or her production ventures, she has left a lasting impact on Indian cinema, earning both critical acclaim and a dedicated audience.

title: Sofiane Feghouli
text:
Sofiane Feghouli was born on December 26, 1989, in Levallois-Perret, a commune in the northwestern suburbs of Paris, France. His parents were Algerian immigrants, with his father hailing from the town of Tlemcen in northwestern Algeria. Feghouli grew up in a working-class family, and from a young age, he displayed a natural talent for football. He began playing organized football at the age of six with local club Red Star FC, based in Saint-Ouen, another suburb of Paris. His skill and dedication quickly set him apart, and by the age of 13, he was scouted by Grenoble Foot 38, a club in southeastern France, where he joined their youth academy in 2003.

Feghouli’s professional career began at Grenoble, where he made his senior debut on May 27, 2007, at the age of 17, in a Ligue 2 match against FC Libourne-Saint-Seurin. The following season, he became a regular in the first team, making 26 appearances and scoring three goals as Grenoble secured promotion to Ligue 1. His performances in the top flight during the 2008-09 season, where he scored five goals in 34 matches, caught the attention of larger clubs. However, Grenoble’s relegation in 2010 and subsequent financial troubles led to his departure.

In June 2010, Feghouli signed a five-year contract with Valencia CF, one of Spain’s most historic clubs, for a reported fee of €4.7 million. His early years at Valencia were marked by inconsistency, as he struggled to secure a starting position under manager Unai Emery. He made his La Liga debut on August 28, 2010, in a 3-0 win over Málaga CF, but managed only 12 league appearances in his first season. A loan move to UD Almería in the 2011-12 season proved pivotal, as he regained form, scoring six goals in 31 Segunda División matches, helping the club narrowly avoid relegation.

Upon returning to Valencia, Feghouli established himself as a key player under new manager Ernesto Valverde. The 2012-13 season was his breakthrough, as he scored 11 goals in 46 appearances across all competitions, including a memorable brace in a 2-0 Europa League win over Lille OSC. His performances earned him the Algerian Footballer of the Year award in 2012, recognizing his contributions to both club and country. Feghouli remained at Valencia until June 2016, making 162 appearances and scoring 23 goals before his contract expired.

In July 2016, Feghouli joined West Ham United on a free transfer, signing a three-year deal. His time in the Premier League was short-lived, as he struggled to adapt to the physicality of English football. He made his debut on August 15, 2016, in a 2-1 defeat to Chelsea, but managed only 18 appearances and one goal before being loaned to Galatasaray in January 2017. His loan was made permanent in June 2017 for a fee of €4.25 million. At Galatasaray, Feghouli found success, winning the Süper Lig title in the 2017-18 and 2018-19 seasons, as well as the Turkish Cup in 2019. He became a fan favorite, scoring 22 goals in 108 appearances over four seasons.

Feghouli’s international career began with France’s youth teams, but he ultimately chose to represent Algeria, making his senior debut on August 29, 2011, in a 2-1 friendly win over Tanzania. He became a crucial player for the Desert Foxes, appearing in three Africa Cup of Nations tournaments (2013, 2015, and 2017) and the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, where he scored Algeria’s first goal in a 2-1 group-stage victory over South Korea. In total, he earned 47 caps and scored 10 goals for Algeria between 2011 and 2021.

After leaving Galatasaray in 2021, Feghouli had a brief stint with Fatih Karagümrük in the Turkish Süper Lig, making 14 appearances before moving to Al-Jazira Club in the UAE Pro League in January 2022. His time in the UAE was short, and by 2023, he returned to Europe, signing with AS Nancy in France’s third-tier Championnat National. Despite his experience, he struggled to make an impact, appearing in only six matches before his contract was terminated in January 2024. As of mid-2024, Feghouli remains a free agent, with his future in football uncertain. Throughout his career, he has been known for his technical ability, versatility as a winger or attacking midfielder, and his leadership on the field.

title: Steve Cummins
text:
Steve Cummins was born on March 12, 1955, in Dublin, Ireland, to parents James Cummins, a civil engineer, and Margaret Cummins (née O’Reilly), a schoolteacher. He grew up in the suburban neighborhood of Rathgar, where he attended St. Conleth’s College, a private Catholic school known for its strong academic and rugby programs. From an early age, Cummins displayed a keen interest in science and sports, particularly rugby, which would later shape his career. He excelled in physics and mathematics, earning top marks in his Leaving Certificate examinations in 1973, which secured him a place at University College Dublin (UCD).

At UCD, Cummins studied mechanical engineering, graduating in 1977 with a first-class honors degree. His academic performance earned him a scholarship to pursue a PhD at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the United States, where he specialized in fluid dynamics and thermodynamics. He completed his doctorate in 1981, publishing his thesis, *"Turbulent Flow in Curved Pipes: A Numerical and Experimental Study,"* which became a foundational work in the field. During his time at MIT, he also played rugby for the university’s club team, further honing his leadership and teamwork skills.

After completing his PhD, Cummins joined the research and development division of General Electric (GE) in Schenectady, New York, in 1982. His work focused on improving the efficiency of gas turbine engines, a critical component in power generation and aviation. Over the next decade, he contributed to several breakthroughs, including the development of the GE90 engine, which debuted in 1995 and became one of the most powerful and fuel-efficient jet engines in the world. His innovations in turbine blade cooling and aerodynamic design earned him 12 patents and the GE Edison Award in 1993, the company’s highest honor for technical achievement.

In 1996, Cummins left GE to become a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom. He was appointed to the prestigious Hopkinson and ICI Professorship of Applied Thermodynamics, a position previously held by notable engineers such as Sir Frank Whittle, the inventor of the jet engine. At Cambridge, he led a research group focused on renewable energy technologies, particularly wind and tidal power. His team’s work on vertical-axis wind turbines resulted in a 20% improvement in efficiency, leading to a collaboration with the British company Vertical Wind Energy Ltd., which commercialized the technology in 2004.

Cummins also played a significant role in public policy, serving as an advisor to the UK government on energy strategy. From 2007 to 2010, he was a member of the Committee on Climate Change, an independent body established under the Climate Change Act 2008 to advise on carbon budgets and emissions targets. His reports, particularly *"The Role of Renewables in the UK’s Energy Mix"* (2009), were instrumental in shaping the government’s renewable energy policies, including the expansion of offshore wind farms. In recognition of his contributions, he was awarded the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2011.

Outside of academia and engineering, Cummins remained an active rugby player and coach. He represented Leinster Rugby at the amateur level in the 1970s and later coached the Cambridge University Rugby Union team from 1998 to 2002, leading them to three consecutive Varsity Match victories against Oxford. His coaching philosophy, which emphasized discipline and innovation, was later documented in his 2005 book, *"The Science of Rugby: How Data and Physics Shape the Game."*

In his later years, Cummins shifted his focus to mentoring young engineers and advocating for sustainable energy solutions. He retired from his professorship at Cambridge in 2015 but continued to serve as a visiting lecturer at Imperial College London and the National University of Ireland, Galway. He also became a trustee of the Engineering Development Trust, a UK charity that promotes engineering careers among students. In 2018, he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, a condition he managed with characteristic determination. He spent his final years in County Wicklow, Ireland, where he lived with his wife, Dr. Fiona Cummins, a pediatrician, whom he had married in 1985. They had two children, Sarah and James. Steve Cummins passed away on November 3, 2022, at the age of 67, leaving behind a legacy of innovation in engineering, education, and sports.

title: Bhuma Nagi Reddy
text:
Bhuma Nagi Reddy was a prominent Indian politician and a key figure in Andhra Pradesh’s political landscape, known for his contributions to the state’s development and his role in the Telugu Desam Party (TDP). Born on 12 December 1964 in the village of Peddapuram in the East Godavari district of Andhra Pradesh, Nagi Reddy hailed from a family with deep political connections. His father, Bhuma Appa Rao, was a local leader and a follower of the Congress party, which influenced Nagi Reddy’s early exposure to politics.

Nagi Reddy completed his schooling in Peddapuram before pursuing higher education at Andhra University in Visakhapatnam, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree. His political career began in the late 1980s when he joined the Telugu Desam Party, founded by the legendary actor-turned-politician N.T. Rama Rao (NTR). Nagi Reddy quickly rose through the ranks due to his organizational skills and grassroots connect, becoming a trusted aide of NTR and later his son-in-law, N. Chandrababu Naidu.

In 1996, Nagi Reddy contested his first Assembly election from the Allagadda constituency in Kurnool district, winning the seat as a TDP candidate. He served as a Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) for three consecutive terms, representing Allagadda in 1999 and 2004 as well. During his tenure, he focused on rural development, irrigation projects, and infrastructure improvements in his constituency. One of his notable achievements was the push for the completion of the Galeru-Nagari Sujala Sravanthi (GNSS) project, a major irrigation scheme aimed at providing water to drought-prone areas in Rayalaseema.

Nagi Reddy’s political influence grew significantly when he was appointed as the Minister for Roads and Buildings in the Andhra Pradesh government in 2004 under Chief Minister Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy’s Congress-led administration. However, his tenure was short-lived due to political realignments, and he later rejoined the TDP. In 2009, he contested the Assembly election from the Nandyal constituency but lost to the Congress candidate. Undeterred, he shifted his focus to the 2014 elections, winning the Nandyal seat with a substantial margin of over 50,000 votes as the TDP returned to power in the newly bifurcated state of Andhra Pradesh.

Following the TDP’s victory in 2014, Nagi Reddy was appointed as the Minister for Endowments in Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu’s cabinet. In this role, he oversaw the administration of Hindu temples and religious institutions, implementing reforms to improve transparency and efficiency. He also played a crucial role in the development of the Yaganti temple in Kurnool district, a major pilgrimage site, by allocating funds for infrastructure upgrades.

Beyond his ministerial duties, Nagi Reddy was known for his philanthropic work, particularly in education and healthcare. He established several schools and hospitals in his constituency, including the Bhuma Nagi Reddy Charitable Trust, which provided scholarships to underprivileged students and free medical camps for rural communities. His efforts earned him a reputation as a leader who prioritized the welfare of his people.

Nagi Reddy’s political career faced challenges in his later years, particularly with the rise of the YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) led by Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy. In the 2019 Assembly elections, he lost the Nandyal seat to the YSRCP candidate, marking a significant setback. Despite this defeat, he remained active in the TDP, advocating for the party’s policies and supporting its candidates in subsequent elections.

Tragically, Bhuma Nagi Reddy’s life was cut short when he passed away on 12 March 2024 at the age of 59 due to a cardiac arrest. His death was mourned by political leaders across parties, who recognized his contributions to Andhra Pradesh’s development. He is survived by his wife, Bhuma Akhila Priya, who is also a politician and served as an MLA and minister in the Andhra Pradesh government, and their two children. Nagi Reddy’s legacy endures through the institutions he built and the policies he championed, leaving an indelible mark on the state’s political and social fabric.

title: Griselda Blanco
text:
Griselda Blanco, known as the "Cocaine Godmother" and the "Black Widow," was one of the most notorious drug lords in history, playing a pivotal role in the rise of the Medellín Cartel during the 1970s and 1980s. Born on February 15, 1943, in Cartagena, Colombia, she grew up in the impoverished neighborhood of Medellín, where she was exposed to crime from an early age. Her mother, Ana Lucía Restrepo, was a strict and abusive figure, while her father, Fernando Blanco, was largely absent. By the age of 11, Blanco was already involved in petty theft and kidnapping, reportedly abducting a child from a wealthy family in Medellín for ransom. The victim was later found dead, marking one of her earliest known violent acts.

Blanco’s criminal career escalated in her teens. At 14, she fled home after stabbing a man who attempted to assault her, and by 19, she had married her first husband, Carlos Trujillo, with whom she had three sons: Dixon, Uber, and Osvaldo. Trujillo was involved in counterfeit money operations, and Blanco quickly adopted his illicit trade. The marriage ended violently when Trujillo was murdered in the early 1970s, allegedly on Blanco’s orders after he became a liability. Around the same time, she married her second husband, Alberto Bravo, a drug trafficker who introduced her to the cocaine trade. Together, they moved to New York City in the mid-1970s, where they established a smuggling network that transported cocaine from Colombia to the U.S. using innovative methods, such as hiding drugs in lingerie and car tires.

By the late 1970s, Blanco’s operation had grown exponentially. She and Bravo smuggled an estimated 1,500 kilograms of cocaine into the U.S. monthly, generating millions in profits. However, their partnership ended in 1975 when Blanco, suspecting Bravo of embezzling money, shot and killed him during a confrontation in Medellín. Following his death, she took full control of the business, expanding her empire with ruthless efficiency. Blanco pioneered the use of motorcycle assassins, known as "sicarios," to carry out hits, a tactic that became a hallmark of her reign. One of her most infamous killings was the 1979 murder of Alfredo "El Padrino" Gómez, a rival drug trafficker, in broad daylight at a Medellín shopping mall. She also ordered the 1982 assassination of two of her own hitmen, Jorge "Rivi" Ayala and Jesús "Chucho" Castro, after they allegedly stole from her.

Blanco’s personal life was as turbulent as her criminal career. In 1978, she married her third husband, Dario Sepúlveda, with whom she had her fourth son, Michael Corleone Blanco, named after the character from *The Godfather*. Their marriage was marked by violence, and Sepúlveda eventually kidnapped Michael during a custody dispute. Blanco responded by ordering Sepúlveda’s murder in 1983, which was carried out by her sicarios in Medellín. By this time, she had relocated to Miami, Florida, where she became a central figure in the city’s cocaine-fueled crime wave. Between 1979 and 1982, Blanco was linked to over 200 murders in Miami-Dade County, including the 1982 Dadeland Mall shooting, where two of her men gunned down two drug dealers in a crowded store.

Despite her brutal reputation, Blanco evaded law enforcement for years. In 1985, she was arrested in Irvine, California, on drug trafficking charges and extradited to New York, where she faced federal indictments. However, she struck a plea deal in 1998, admitting to three murders in exchange for a reduced sentence. She was sentenced to 20 years in prison but served only six before being deported to Colombia in 2004. Upon her return, she lived relatively quietly in Medellín, though rumors persisted of her continued involvement in the drug trade.

Blanco’s life came to a violent end on September 3, 2012, when she was shot twice in the head by an unknown assailant while leaving a butcher shop in Medellín. She was 69 years old. Her death remains shrouded in mystery, with theories ranging from retaliation by rival cartels to a hit ordered by former associates. At the time of her death, Blanco’s net worth was estimated at $2 billion, though much of it had been seized by authorities. Her legacy endures in pop culture, with documentaries, books, and the 2022 Netflix series *Griselda* dramatizing her life. Despite her infamy, she remains a complex figure—a woman who rose from poverty to become one of the most feared criminals of her time, leaving behind a trail of bloodshed and a lasting impact on the global drug trade.

title: Jimmy Weldon
text:
Jimmy Weldon was born James Weldon on September 23, 1923, in Dallas, Texas. He grew up in a working-class family, the son of James Weldon Sr., a mechanic, and Mary Weldon, a homemaker. From an early age, Weldon displayed a keen interest in performing, particularly in ventriloquism and comedy. His fascination with puppetry began when he received a ventriloquist dummy as a gift at the age of 12, which he named "Webster." This early exposure to entertainment set the stage for his future career.

After graduating from high school in 1941, Weldon enlisted in the U.S. Army during World War II, serving as a radio operator in the Pacific Theater. His military service lasted until 1945, when he was honorably discharged. Following the war, he used the G.I. Bill to attend the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York City, where he studied acting and honed his skills in voice work and comedy. During this time, he also performed in local theaters and nightclubs, gradually building a reputation as a talented ventriloquist.

In the late 1940s, Weldon began appearing on radio programs, including *The Jimmy Weldon Show*, a local broadcast in New York that showcased his ventriloquism and comedic timing. His big break came in 1950 when he was cast as the voice of "Yakky Doodle," a cartoon duck, in the Hanna-Barbera animated series *The Yogi Bear Show*. The character debuted in 1961 and became one of Weldon’s most recognizable roles, running for 33 episodes until 1962. His high-pitched, nasally voice for Yakky Doodle became iconic, and the character remained a staple in Hanna-Barbera’s reruns for decades.

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Weldon worked extensively in television and voice acting. He provided voices for other Hanna-Barbera characters, including "Touche Turtle" in *Touche Turtle and Dum Dum* (1962–1963) and various roles in *The Flintstones* and *The Jetsons*. His versatility extended beyond animation; he appeared as a guest on popular variety shows such as *The Ed Sullivan Show* (1950s–1960s) and *The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson* (1960s–1970s), where he performed his ventriloquism act. In 1964, he published a book titled *Ventriloquism for Fun and Profit*, which became a popular guide for aspiring ventriloquists.

Weldon’s career also included live performances, where he toured the United States and internationally with his ventriloquist act. He was known for his ability to engage audiences with his dummy, Webster, who often delivered sharp, humorous commentary. In the 1970s, he appeared in commercials, including a memorable campaign for Kellogg’s Frosted Flakes, where he voiced Tony the Tiger’s friend, "Katy the Kangaroo." His work in advertising extended to other brands, such as McDonald’s and Coca-Cola, further cementing his status as a versatile voice actor.

In addition to his entertainment career, Weldon was a dedicated educator. He conducted workshops and seminars on ventriloquism and voice acting, sharing his expertise with aspiring performers. In 1980, he founded the International Ventriloquist Society, an organization that promoted the art of ventriloquism and provided resources for performers. The society grew to include hundreds of members worldwide and hosted annual conventions where Weldon often served as a keynote speaker.

Weldon’s later years were marked by continued involvement in entertainment and education. He made occasional appearances at nostalgia conventions and voice acting panels, where he shared stories from his career. In 2004, he was honored with a Lifetime Achievement Award by the International Ventriloquist Society for his contributions to the art form. Despite retiring from regular performances, he remained active in mentoring young ventriloquists and occasionally lent his voice to projects, including a 2010 revival of *Yogi Bear* in which he reprised his role as Yakky Doodle.

Jimmy Weldon passed away on January 14, 2023, at the age of 99, in his home in Los Angeles, California. He was survived by his wife of 65 years, Barbara Weldon, whom he married in 1958, and their two children, James Weldon III and Jennifer Weldon. His legacy endures through his extensive body of work in animation, television, and live performance, as well as his contributions to the art of ventriloquism. Weldon’s career spanned over seven decades, leaving an indelible mark on the entertainment industry.

title: Theophilus Annorbaah
text:
Theophilus Annorbaah was a Ghanaian agricultural scientist and academic whose work significantly contributed to crop improvement and food security in West Africa. Born on June 15, 1952, in the small farming community of Akim Oda in the Eastern Region of Ghana, Annorbaah grew up in a family deeply connected to agriculture. His parents, Kwame Annorbaah and Akosua Serwaa, were subsistence farmers who cultivated cassava, maize, and plantains, instilling in him an early appreciation for farming and the challenges faced by smallholder farmers in the region.

Annorbaah attended Akim Oda Local Authority Primary School from 1958 to 1964, where he excelled in science and mathematics.
